$$

$$

questions.knowledge_point: Differentiating a Negative Power Function Using the Constant Multiple Rule
questions.problem: If $y=\frac{1}{4x},$ find $\frac{dy}{dx}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We first rewrite the function as

$$
y=\frac{1}{4x}=\frac{1}{4}{x}^{-1}.
$$

Then, we apply the constant multiple and power rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{d}{dx}(\frac{1}{4}{x}^{-1}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{-1}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot (-1){x}^{-1-1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{-2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Differentiating a Sum of Functions Without Constant Factors Using the Sum Rule
questions.problem: Find ${f}^{'}(x)$ for  $f(x)={x}^{2}+x-\sqrt{x}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The function $f(x)$ is the sum of three power functions. So, we apply the sum rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+x-\sqrt{x}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sqrt{x}) \\  & =2{x}^{(2-1)}+1-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{1/2-1} \\  & =2x+1-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-1/2} \\  & =2x-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Factoring a Polynomial With Leading Coefficients as a Difference of Squares
questions.problem: Factor the expression $2{r}^{4}-32.$
questions.worked_solution:
The difference of squares formula is given by

$$
{a}^{2}-{b}^{2}=(a+b)(a-b)
$$

Notice that all of the terms in our expression have a common factor of $2.$ To simplify the computation, we can factor out the $2,$ as follows:

$$
2{r}^{4}-32=2\cdot {r}^{4}-2\cdot 16=2({r}^{4}-16)
$$

The expression in parentheses can be written as a difference of squares:

$$
2({r}^{4}-16)=2({({r}^{2})}^{2}-{4}^{2})
$$

Now, we factor our expression using the difference of squares formula:

$$
2({({r}^{2})}^{2}-{4}^{2})=2({r}^{2}+4)({r}^{2}-4)
$$

Finally, we notice that the expression in the second set of parentheses is also a difference of squares. Therefore, the expression can be factored further, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2({r}^{2}+4)({r}^{2}-4) & =2({r}^{2}+4)({r}^{2}-{2}^{2}) \\  & =2({r}^{2}+4)(r+2)(r-2)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Applying the Power Rule to Compute a Limit Given a Graph
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/history-question-import-2026-10-04/import-ready/assets/a086a1f616aee596a021ee4ef6bdc8723309cf8959719e9f55d6f20b845bd760.png)

If the figure above shows the graph of the function $f(x),$ then

${lim}_{x\to -2}({x}^{2}+3)^{2}(5-f(x))^{3}=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
From the graph we get that ${lim}_{x\to -2}f(x)=4.$ 

From the product rule, we have

$$
{lim}_{x\to -2}({x}^{2}+3)^{2}(5-f(x))^{3}={lim}_{x\to -2}({x}^{2}+3)^{2}\cdot {lim}_{x\to -2}(5-f(x))^{3}.
$$

We calculate the limits of each factor, separately.

Applying the power rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -2}({x}^{2}+3)^{2} & ={({lim}_{x\to -2}({x}^{2}+3))}^{2} \\  & ={((-2)^{2}+3)}^{2} \\  & ={(4+3)}^{2} \\  & ={7}^{2} \\  & =49\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -2}(5-f(x))^{3} & ={({lim}_{x\to -2}(5-f(x)))}^{3} \\  & ={(5-4)}^{3} \\  & ={1}^{3} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -2}({x}^{2}+3)^{2}(5-f(x))^{3} & =49\cdot 1 \\  & =49.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Terms of a Fibonacci Sequence Given in Function Notation
questions.problem:
The recursive formula for the Fibonacci numbers is 

$$
f(n+2)=f(n+1)+f(n),\,f(1)=f(2)=1,\,n\ge 1.
$$

The $6$th term of the sequence is{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
The recursion relation is

$$
f(n+2)=f(n+1)+f(n).
$$

Substituting $n=1$ into the recursive formula gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1+2) & =f(1+1)+f(1) \\ f(3) & =f(2)+f(1) \\ f(3) & =1+1 \\ f(3) & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, substituting $n=2,3,4$ into the recursive formula gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(4) & =f(2+2)=f(2+1)+f(2)=f(3)+f(2)=2+1=3 \\ f(5) & =f(3+2)=f(3+1)+f(3)=f(4)+f(3)=3+2=5 \\ f(6) & =f(4+2)=f(4+1)+f(4)=f(5)+f(4)=5+3=8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $6$th term of the sequence is $8.$

questions.knowledge_point: Rearranging and Solving a Quadratic Equation With Complex Roots
questions.problem: Solve the equation $\,{x}^{2}+2x=-50.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write the equation in standard form by bringing all of the terms to the left-hand side. This gives the equation

$$
{x}^{2}+2x+50=0.
$$

We can find the roots of a quadratic equation using the quadratic formula:

$$
x=\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a}
$$

In this case, the coefficients are $a=1,\,b=2,$ and $c=50.$ Substituting these values into the quadratic formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{-2\pm \sqrt{{2}^{2}-4(1)(50)}}{2(1)} \\  & =\frac{-2\pm \sqrt{4-200}}{2} \\  & =\frac{-2\pm \sqrt{-196}}{2} \\  & =\frac{-2\pm 14\,\text{i}}{2} \\  & =-1\pm 7\,\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation has two solutions, $x=-1+7\,\text{i}$ and $x=-1-7\,\text{i}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Multiplicity of a Root of a Cubic Polynomial Using Synthetic Division
questions.problem: The multiplicity of the root $x=-5$ in the polynomial $p(x)={x}^{3}+6{x}^{2}-15x-100$ is{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Since $x=-5$ is a root of $p(x),$ the factor theorem tells us that $(x+5)$ is a factor of $p(x).$

Because $(x+5)$ is a factor of $p(x),$ we know that $(x+5)$ divides $p(x)$ with no remainder. So, to begin factoring $p(x),$ we can divide it by $(x+5)$ using synthetic division:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $-5$ | $1$ | $6$ | $-15$ | $-100$ |
|  | $↓$ | $-5$ | $-5$ | $100$ |
|  | $1$ | $1$ | $-20$ | $0$ |

Therefore,

$$
\frac{p(x)}{x+5}={x}^{2}+x-20,
$$

which means that

$$
p(x)=(x+5)({x}^{2}+x-20).
$$

We can factor the quadratic factor even further, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}p(x) & =(x+5)(x-4)(x+5) \\  & =(x-4)(x+5)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The factor $(x+5)$ has an exponent of $2$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=-5$ has multiplicity $2.$

$$
\begin{aligned}9-3x & =0 \\ -3x & =-9 \\ x & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the vertical asymptote is $x=3.$

questions.problem: Rio's Pizza offers a mix and match pizza on its menu. There are $4$ different meat types to choose from, $5$ different vegetables, $4$ different types of cheese, and $2$ different types of crust. How many different types of pizza can be made by choosing a type of meat, a vegetable, cheese and a crust?
questions.worked_solution:
Using the **rule of product**, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Number of pizzas} & =\text{Number of type of meats} \\  & \times \text{Number of type of vegetables} \\  & \times \text{Number of type of cheese} \\  & \times \text{Number of type of crust} \\  & =4\times 5\times 4\times 2 \\  & =160.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $160$ types of pizza can be made with the given ingredients.

questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Multiplicity of a Root of a Cubic Polynomial Using Grouping
questions.problem: Which root(s) of the polynomial $p(x)=2{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}+32x+16$ have multiplicity $2?$
questions.worked_solution:
We factor the cubic by grouping, and simplify until the polynomial is fully factored:

$$
\begin{aligned}p(x) & =2{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}+32x+16 \\  & ={x}^{2}(2x+1)+16(2x+1) \\  & =({x}^{2}+16)(2x+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the factor $({x}^{2}+16)$ cannot be factored any further, and it does not have any real roots.

The only real root of $p(x)$ comes from the factor $(2x+1).$ This factor has a root of $x=-\frac{1}{2},$ and the exponent of the factor is $1.$ Therefore, the root $x=-\frac{1}{2}$ has multiplicity $1.$

In conclusion, there is no root with multiplicity $2.$

$$
\begin{aligned}p(x) & =5{x}^{3}-15{x}^{2} \\  & =5{x}^{2}(x-3)\end{aligned}
$$

To find the roots and their multiplicities, we look at the factors:

- The factor $x$ has an exponent of $2$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=0$ has multiplicity $2.$

- The factor $(x-3)$ has an exponent of $1$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=3$ has multiplicity $1.$

In conclusion, only the root $x=0$ has multiplicity $2.$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Multiplicity of a Root of a Cubic Polynomial Using Synthetic Division
questions.problem: The multiplicity of the root $x=1$ in the polynomial $p(x)={x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}-11x+6$ is{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Since $x=1$ is a root of $p(x),$ the factor theorem tells us that $(x-1)$ is a factor of $p(x).$

Because $(x-1)$ is a factor of $p(x),$ we know that $(x-1)$ divides $p(x)$ with no remainder. So, to begin factoring $p(x),$ we can divide it by $(x-1)$ using synthetic division:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $1$ | $4$ | $-11$ | $6$ |
|  | $↓$ | $1$ | $5$ | $-6$ |
|  | $1$ | $5$ | $-6$ | $0$ |

Therefore,

$$
\frac{p(x)}{x-1}={x}^{2}+5x-6,
$$

which means that

$$
p(x)=(x-1)({x}^{2}+5x-6).
$$

We can factor the quadratic factor even further, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}p(x) & =(x-1)(x-1)(x+6) \\  & =(x+6)(x-1)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The factor $(x-1)$ has an exponent of $2$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=1$ has multiplicity $2.$

questions.knowledge_point: Factoring a Polynomial With Leading Coefficients as a Difference of Squares
questions.problem: Factor $243-3{x}^{4}$ completely.
questions.worked_solution:
The difference of squares formula is given by

$$
{a}^{2}-{b}^{2}=(a+b)(a-b)
$$

Notice that all of the terms have a common factor of $3.$ To simplify the computation, we can factor out the $3,$ as follows:

$$
243-3{x}^{4}=3\cdot 81-3\cdot {x}^{4}=3(81-{x}^{4})
$$

The expression in parentheses can be written as a difference of squares:

$$
3(81-{x}^{4})=3({9}^{2}-{({x}^{2})}^{2})
$$

Now, we factor our expression using the difference of squares formula:

$$
3({9}^{2}-{({x}^{2})}^{2})=3(9+{x}^{2})(9-{x}^{2})
$$

Finally, we notice that the expression in the second set of parentheses is also a difference of squares. Therefore, the expression can be factored further, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3(9+{x}^{2})(9-{x}^{2}) & =3(9+{x}^{2})({3}^{2}-{x}^{2}) \\  & =3(9+{x}^{2})(3+x)(3-x)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Terms of a Fibonacci Sequence Given in Function Notation
questions.worked_solution:
The recursion relation is

$$
f(n+2)=f(n+1)+f(n).
$$

Substituting $n=1$ into the recursive formula gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1+2) & =f(1+1)+f(1) \\ f(3) & =f(2)+f(1) \\ f(3) & =5+0 \\ f(3) & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $n=2$ into the recursive formula gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2+2) & =f(2+1)+f(2) \\ f(4) & =f(3)+f(2) \\ f(4) & =5+5 \\ f(4) & =10\end{aligned}
$$

We continue this process to compute $f(5)$ and $f(6)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(5) & =f(3+2)=f(3+1)+f(3)=f(4)+f(3)=10+5=15 \\ f(6) & =f(4+2)=f(4+1)+f(4)=f(5)+f(4)=15+10=25\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f(6)=25.$

questions.knowledge_point: Rearranging and Solving a Quadratic Equation With Complex Roots
questions.problem: Solve the equation $\,-6x=-{x}^{2}-13.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write the equation in standard form by bringing all of the terms to the left-hand side. This gives the equation

$$
{x}^{2}-6x+13=0.
$$

We can find the roots of a quadratic equation using the quadratic formula:

$$
x=\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a}
$$

In this case, the coefficients are $a=1,\,b=-6,$ and $c=13.$ Substituting these values into the quadratic formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{-(-6)\pm \sqrt{(-6)^{2}-4(1)(13)}}{2(1)} \\  & =\frac{6\pm \sqrt{36-52}}{2} \\  & =\frac{6\pm \sqrt{-16}}{2} \\  & =\frac{6\pm 4\,\text{i}}{2} \\  & =3\pm 2\,\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation has two solutions, $x=3+2\,\text{i}$ and $x=3-2\,\text{i}.$

questions.problem: What is the multiplicity of the root $x=-2$ in the polynomial $p(x)={x}^{3}+8{x}^{2}+20x+16?$
questions.worked_solution:

Because $(x+2)$ is a factor of $p(x),$ we know that $(x+2)$ divides $p(x)$ with no remainder. So, to begin factoring $p(x),$ we can divide it by $(x+2)$ using synthetic division:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |

| $-2$ | $1$ | $8$ | $20$ | $16$ |
|  | $↓$ | $-2$ | $-12$ | $-16$ |
|  | $1$ | $6$ | $8$ | $0$ |

Therefore,

$$
\frac{p(x)}{x+2}={x}^{2}+6x+8,
$$

which means that

$$
p(x)=(x+2)({x}^{2}+6x+8).
$$

We can factor the quadratic factor even further, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}p(x) & =(x+2)(x+2)(x+4) \\  & =(x+4)(x+2)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The factor $(x+2)$ has an exponent of $2$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=-2$ has multiplicity $2.$

questions.worked_solution:

questions.problem: Calculate $\int \frac{1}{2{y}^{5}}\,\text{d}y.$
questions.worked_solution:
We can just take the constant factor out of the integral, and then apply the power rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{2{y}^{5}}\,\text{d}y & =\frac{1}{2}\int {y}^{-5}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (\frac{{y}^{-5+1}}{-5+1})+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (\frac{{y}^{-4}}{-4})+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{8}\cdot {y}^{-4}+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{8{y}^{4}}+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Applying the Rule of Product
questions.problem: How many possible outcomes are there if a coin is flipped twice, a six-sided die is rolled three times, and a tetrahedral (four-sided) die is rolled once?
questions.worked_solution:
For the coin, there are $2$ outcomes: "Heads" and "Tails".

For the six-sided die, there is a total of $6$ outcomes: $1,2,3,4,5,6.$

For the tetrahedral die, there is a total of $4$ outcomes: $1,2,3,4.$

Using the **rule of product**, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Total Possible Outcomes} & =\text{Number of outcomes when the coin is flipped the first time} \\  & \times \text{Number of outcomes when the coin is flipped the second time} \\  & \times \text{Number of outcomes when the six-sided die is rolled the first time} \\  & \times \text{Number of outcomes when the six-sided die is rolled the second time} \\  & \times \text{Number of outcomes when the six-sided die is rolled the third time} \\  & \times \text{Number of outcomes when the tetrahedral die is rolled the one time} \\  & =2\times 2\times 6\times 6\times 6\times 4 \\  & ={2}^{2}\times {6}^{3}\times 4 \\  & =4\times 216\times 4 \\  & =3\,456.\end{aligned}
$$

So, there are $3\,456$ possible outcomes.

questions.problem:
Find, in radians, the argument of $z=-2+2\text{i}.$ 

**Hint**: The argument of a complex number is in the range $[0,2\pi ).$
questions.worked_solution:

The complex number $z$ lies in the second quadrant of the complex plane. Therefore $\frac{\pi }{2}<\operatorname{arg}(z)<\pi .$ If $\alpha $ is the angle that $z$ makes with the negative real axis, then

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}\alpha  & =\frac{2}{2} \\ \alpha  & =\operatorname{arctan}(1) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arg}(z)=\pi -\frac{\pi }{4}=\frac{3\pi }{4}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Possible Roots of a Polynomial Using the Rational Roots Theorem
questions.problem: According to the rational roots theorem, which of the following could be a root of the polynomial $f(x)=4{x}^{7}-12{x}^{4}+5{x}^{2}-3x+10?$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, the rational roots theorem states that any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of the constant term}}{\text{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

For the given polynomial $f(x),$ the constant term is $10,$ and the leading coefficient is $4.$ So, any rational roots of $f(x)$ must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of }10}{\text{factor of }4}.
$$

Of the given answer choices, only $\frac{5}{4}$ takes the above form since the numerator $(5)$ is a factor of $10$ and the denominator $(4)$ is a factor of $4.$

questions.worked_solution:
Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, the rational roots theorem states that any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of the constant term}}{\text{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

For the given polynomial $f(x),$ the constant term is $-3$ and the leading coefficient is $2.$ So, any rational roots of $f(x)$ must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of }-3}{\text{factor of }2}.
$$

Of the given answer choices, only $2$ does not take the above form. The value $2$ can be interpreted as a fraction $\frac{2}{1},$ and the numerator $(2)$ is not a factor of $-3.$

questions.knowledge_point: Counting the Number of Possible Rational Roots of a Polynomial
questions.problem: According to the rational root theorem, the polynomial $f(x)=25{x}^{3}+6{x}^{2}-x-5$ has{{field-1}} *potential* rational roots.
questions.worked_solution:
Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, the rational roots theorem states that any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of the constant term}}{\text{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

For the given polynomial:

- The constant term is $-5,$ and its factors are $\pm 1$ and $\pm 5.$

- The leading coefficient is $25,$ and its factors are $\pm 1$, $\pm 5$, and $\pm 25.$

First, we list out all the possibilities for the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\pm \frac{1}{1},\text{ }\pm \frac{1}{5},\text{ }\pm \frac{1}{25}, \\ \pm \frac{5}{1},\text{ }\pm \frac{5}{5},\text{ }\pm \frac{5}{25}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we reduce the fractions to their lowest terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\pm 1,\text{ }\pm \frac{1}{5},\text{ }\pm \frac{1}{25}, \\ \pm 5,\text{ }\pm 1,\text{ }\pm \frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that some potential roots are duplicates (shown above in red). Removing these duplicates and listing those remaining in order from least to greatest in absolute value, we have

$$
\pm \frac{1}{25},\,\pm \frac{1}{5},\,\pm 1,\,\pm 5.
$$

This makes a total of $8$ potential roots. (Remember that each $\pm $ sign accounts for $2$ roots, and $2\cdot 4=8.$)

questions.knowledge_point: Counting the Number of Possible Rational Roots of a Polynomial
questions.problem: For the polynomial $f(x)=5{x}^{3}+2{x}^{2}-x+12,$ how many *potential* roots are given by the rational roots theorem?
questions.worked_solution:
Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, the rational roots theorem states that any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of the constant term}}{\text{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

For the given polynomial:

- The constant term is $12,$ and its factors are $\pm 1,\,\pm 2,\,\pm 3,\,\pm 4,\,\pm 6$ and $\pm 12.$

- The leading coefficient is $5,$ and its factors are $\pm 1$ and $\pm 5.$

First, we list out all the possibilities for the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\pm \frac{1}{1}, & \pm \frac{1}{5}, \\ \pm \frac{2}{1}, & \pm \frac{2}{5}, \\ \pm \frac{3}{1}, & \pm \frac{3}{5}, \\ \pm \frac{4}{1}, & \pm \frac{4}{5}, \\ \pm \frac{6}{1}, & \pm \frac{6}{5}, \\ \pm \frac{12}{1}, & \pm \frac{12}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we reduce the fractions to lowest terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\pm 1, & \pm \frac{1}{5}, \\ \pm 2, & \pm \frac{2}{5}, \\ \pm 3, & \pm \frac{3}{5}, \\ \pm 4, & \pm \frac{4}{5}, \\ \pm 6, & \pm \frac{6}{5}, \\ \pm 12, & \pm \frac{12}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that none of these potential roots are duplicates. Listing those potential roots in order from least to greatest in absolute value, we have

$$
\pm \frac{1}{5},\,\pm \frac{2}{5},\,\pm \frac{3}{5},\,\pm \frac{4}{5},\,\pm 1\,\pm \frac{6}{5},\,\pm 2,\,\pm \frac{12}{5},\,\pm 3,\,\pm 4,\,\pm 6,\,\pm 12.
$$

This makes a total of $24$ potential roots. (Remember that each $\pm $ sign accounts for $2$ roots, and $2\cdot 12=24.$)

questions.knowledge_point: Factoring a Cubic Polynomial Using the Rational Roots Theorem
questions.problem: Given that the polynomial $f(x)=27{x}^{3}-54{x}^{2}+36x-8$ has a root in the interval $(\frac{1}{2},1),$ the sum of the **distinct** real roots of $f(x)$ equals{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, the rational roots theorem states that any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of the constant term}}{\text{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

For the given polynomial $f(x),$ the constant term is $-8$ and the leading coefficient is $27.$ So, any rational roots of $f(x)$ must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of }-8}{\text{factor of }27}.
$$

Therefore, the possible rational roots are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned} & \pm \frac{1}{27},\,\pm \frac{2}{27},\,\pm \frac{1}{9},\,\pm \frac{4}{27},\,\pm \frac{2}{9},\,\frac{8}{27},\,\pm \frac{1}{3},\,\pm \frac{4}{9}, \\  & \pm \frac{2}{3},\,\pm \frac{8}{9},\,\pm 1,\,\pm \frac{4}{3},\,\pm 2,\,\pm \frac{8}{3},\,\pm 4,\,\pm 8\end{aligned}
$$

Of these roots, the only roots in the interval $(\frac{1}{2},1)$ are $\frac{2}{3}$ and $\frac{8}{9}.$

Now, let's use synthetic division to test whether $(x-\frac{2}{3})$ is a factor of $f(x).$ We get the following:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\frac{2}{3}$ | $27$ | $-54$ | $36$ | $-8$ |
|  | $↓$ | $18$ | $-24$ | $8$ |
|  | $27$ | $-36$ | $12$ | $0$ |

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(x-\frac{2}{3})(27{x}^{2}-36x+12).\end{aligned}
$$

Since the highest-degree factor is now a quadratic, we can continue factoring using the usual methods:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(x-\frac{2}{3})(27{x}^{2}-36x+12) \\  & =3(x-\frac{2}{3})(9{x}^{2}-12x+4) \\  & =3(x-\frac{2}{3})(3x-2)^{2} \\  & =(3x-2)(3x-2)^{2} \\  & =(3x-2)^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the only root of $f(x)$ is $x=\frac{2}{3}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Factoring a Cubic Polynomial Using the Rational Roots Theorem
questions.problem: Given that the polynomial $f(x)={x}^{3}+{x}^{2}-10x+8$ has one of its roots in the interval $(-5,-1),$ find the sum of the distinct real roots of $f(x).$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, the rational roots theorem states that any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of the constant term}}{\text{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

For the given polynomial $f(x),$ the constant term is $8$ and the leading coefficient is $1.$ So, any rational roots of $f(x)$ must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of }8}{\text{factor of }1}.
$$

Therefore, the possible rational roots are as follows:

$$
\pm 1,\pm 2,\pm 4,\pm 8
$$

Of these roots, the only roots in the interval $(-5,-1),$ are $-4$ and $-2.$

Now, let's use synthetic division to test whether $(x+4)$ is a factor of $f(x).$ We get the following:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $-4$ | $1$ | $1$ | $-10$ | $8$ |
|  | $↓$ | $-4$ | $12$ | $-8$ |
|  | $1$ | $-3$ | $2$ | $0$ |

Since the highest-degree factor is now a quadratic, we can continue factoring using the usual methods:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(x+4)({x}^{2}-3x+2) \\  & =(x+4)(x-1)(x-2)\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the factors equal to $0,$ we find the roots $x=-4,1,2.$ Summing these roots, we get

$$
-4+1+2=-1.
$$

questions.problem:
The polynomial $f(x)={x}^{3}+3{x}^{2}-10x-24$ has one of its roots in the interval $(2,4).$ In **ascending order**, the distinct real roots of $f(x)$ are

$x=$
{{field-1}}$,\,x=$
{{field-2}}$,\,x=$

questions.worked_solution:
Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, the rational roots theorem states that any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of the constant term}}{\text{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

For the given polynomial $f(x),$ the constant term is $-24$ and the leading coefficient is $1.$ So, any rational roots of $f(x)$ must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of }-24}{\text{factor of }1}.
$$

Therefore, the possible rational roots are as follows:

$$
\pm 1,\,\pm 2,\,\pm 3,\,\pm 4,\,\pm 6,\,\pm 8,\,\pm 12,\,\pm 24.
$$

Of these roots, the only root in the interval $(2,4)$ is $3.$

Now, let's use synthetic division to test whether $(x-3)$ is a factor of $f(x).$ We get the following:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $3$ | $1$ | $3$ | $-10$ | $-24$ |
|  | $↓$ | $3$ | $18$ | $24$ |
|  | $1$ | $6$ | $8$ | $0$ |

Since the remainder is $0,$ we conclude that $(x-3)$ is indeed a factor of $f(x).$ Moreover, we have

$$
f(x)=(x-3)({x}^{2}+6x+8).
$$

Since the highest-degree factor is now a quadratic, we can continue factoring using the usual methods:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(x-3)({x}^{2}+6x+8) \\  & =(x-3)(x+2)(x+4).\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the factors equal to $0,$ we find that, in ascending order, the roots of the polynomial are $x=-4,$ $x=-2,$ and $x=3.$

questions.problem:
Find, **in radians**, the argument of $z=-7+5\text{i}.$ Round your final answer to **two decimal places**.

**Hint**: The argument of a complex number is in the range $[0,2\pi ).$

The complex number $z$ lies in the second quadrant of the complex plane. Hence $\frac{\pi }{2}<\operatorname{arg}(z)<\pi .$ 

If $\alpha $ is the angle that $z$ makes with the negative real axis, then

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}\alpha  & =\frac{5}{7} \\ \alpha  & =\operatorname{arctan}(\frac{5}{7}) \\  & =0.620\text{ }249\text{ }…\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arg}(z)=\pi -0.620\text{ }249\text{ }…\approx 2.52,
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/history-question-import-2026-10-04/import-ready/assets/a058d9b800decdb32fdd09715f1bebab03b4a12c7e6119d6c45bbb170ce640b0.png)

What is the length of $\overset{―}{PQ}$ in the diagram above?
questions.worked_solution:
The length of $\overset{―}{AB}$ is equal to the distance between $P$ and $Q.$

The distance $d$ between two points $P({x}_{1},{y}_{1},{z}_{1})$ and $Q({x}_{2},{y}_{2},{z}_{2})$ is given by

$$
d=\sqrt{({x}_{2}-{x}_{1})^{2}+({y}_{2}-{y}_{1})^{2}+({z}_{2}-{z}_{1})^{2}}.
$$

Since $P$ and $Q$ have coordinates ${{(6,\,0,\,1)}_{⏟}}_{\text{(}{x}_{1}\text{, }{y}_{1}\text{, }{z}_{1}\text{)}}$ and ${{(-1,4,2)}_{⏟}}_{\text{(}{x}_{2}\text{, }{y}_{2}\text{, }{z}_{2}\text{)}},$ respectively, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}PQ & =\sqrt{(-1-6)^{2}+(4-0)^{2}+(2-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-7)^{2}+{4}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{66}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Sum of the Roots of a Quadratic Equation
questions.problem:
Consider the quadratic equation

$$
7{x}^{2}-9x+2=0.
$$

**Without** solving the equation, determine the sum of its solutions.
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose the quadratic equation

$$
a{x}^{2}+bx+c=0
$$

has the solutions $x={x}_{1}$ and $x={x}_{2},$ where $a\ne 0.$ 

Then, Vieta's formulas state the following:

- The sum of the solutions is given by

$$
{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=-\frac{b}{a}.
$$

- The product of the solutions is given by

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=\frac{c}{a}.
$$

For the given quadratic equation, we have

$$
a=7,\,b=-9,\,c=2.
$$

Therefore, the sum of the solutions is

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{b}{a} & =-\frac{(-9)}{7}=\frac{9}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Suppose the quadratic equation

$$
a{x}^{2}+bx+c=0
$$

has the solutions $x={x}_{1}$ and $x={x}_{2},$ where $a\ne 0.$ 

Then, Vieta's formulas state the following:

- The sum of the solutions is given by

$$
{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=-\frac{b}{a}.
$$

- The product of the solutions is given by

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=\frac{c}{a}.
$$

Now, let's use the given information to determine the values of $a,b,$ and $c$ in this case:

- We're told that the quadratic coefficient equals $1.$ Therefore, we have

$$
a=1.
$$

- We're told that the sum of the roots equals $-11.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-11 & =-\frac{b}{a} \\ -11 & =-\frac{b}{1} \\ 11 & =b \\ b & =11.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}-28 & =\frac{c}{a} \\ -28 & =\frac{c}{1} \\ c & =-28.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
a=1,\,b=11,\,c=-28
$$

and the equation is

$$
{x}^{2}+11x-28=0.

questions.problem: Given that $\frac{3}{2z}=p$ and $\frac{2}{z}=q,$ what is $p-q?$
questions.worked_solution:
We wish to subtract the following fractions:

$$
p-q=\frac{3}{2z}-\frac{2}{z}
$$

In order to subtract the two fractions, we need them to have a common denominator. Here, we can put both fractions over a common denominator of $2z$ if we multiply the top and bottom of the second fraction by $2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2z}-\frac{2}{z} & = \\ \frac{3}{2z}-\frac{2}{2}\cdot \frac{2}{z} & = \\ \frac{3}{2z}-\frac{4}{2z} & = \\ \frac{3-4}{2z} & = \\ -\frac{1}{2z} & \end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Adding Rational Expressions in One Variable With Common Factors in the Denominators
questions.problem: If $\frac{p-2}{p+2}+X=\frac{2p}{3p+6},$ then what is $X?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $\frac{p-2}{p+2}+X=\frac{2p}{3p+6},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}X & =\frac{2p}{3p+6}-\frac{p-2}{p+2} \\  & =\frac{2p}{3(p+2)}-\frac{p-2}{p+2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In order to add the two fractions, we need them to have a common denominator. Here, we can put both fractions over a common denominator of $3(p+2)$ if we multiply the top and bottom of the second fraction by $3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}X & =\frac{2p}{3(p+2)}-\frac{p-2}{p+2} \\  & =\frac{2p}{3(p+2)}-\frac{3}{3}\cdot \frac{p-2}{p+2} \\  & =\frac{2p}{3(p+2)}-\frac{3(p-2)}{3(p+2)} \\  & =\frac{2p-3(p-2)}{3(p+2)} \\  & =\frac{2p-3p+6}{3(p+2)} \\  & =\frac{-p+6}{3(p+2)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore $X=\frac{-p+6}{3(p+2)}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving Two-Step Equations
questions.worked_solution:
In part 1, we found that $p(20)=400a+20b.$ So, we need to solve the equation $400a+20b=4\,800$ for the parameter $b.$

We need to isolate the variable $b.$ To do this, we treat $a$ as though it were a constant and apply the addition and multiplication principles as usual.

First, we subtract $400a$ from both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}400a+20b & =4\,800 \\ 400a+20b-400a & =4\,800-400a \\ 20b & =4\,800-400a\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we divide both sides of the equation by $20:$

$$
\begin{aligned}20b & =4\,800-400a \\ \frac{20b}{20} & =\frac{4\,800-400a}{20} \\ \frac{\cancel{20}b}{\cancel{20}} & =\frac{4\,800}{20}-\frac{400a}{20} \\ b & =240-20a\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $b=240-20a.$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving a System of Linear Equations Using Substitution
questions.worked_solution:
We have the following system of linear equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}b=240-20a \\ 30b+900a=6\,000\end{aligned}
$$

We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. 

Notice that the first equation is already solved for $b:$

$$
b=240-20a
$$

So, we replace $b$ in the second equation and solve for $a:$

$$
\begin{aligned}30b+900a & =6\,000 \\ 30(240-20a)+900a & =6\,000 \\ 7\,200-600a+900a & =6\,000 \\ 7\,200+300a & =6\,000 \\ 300a & =-1\,200 \\ a & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute $a=-4$ into $b=240-20a,$ we can then find the value of $b:$

$$
\begin{aligned}b & =240-20(-4) \\ b & =320\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $a=-4,\,b=320.$

questions.problem:
The manager wants to determine the number of cakes the bakery should produce per week to make a weekly profit of $$6\,000.$ The required number of cakes $x$ is the solution to the equation

$$
4{x}^{2}-320x+6\,000=0.
$$

This equation can be factored as $\,$$4\cdot ($
{{field-1}} $)=0.$
questions.worked_solution:
We factor $4{x}^{2}-320x+6\,000$ using the greatest common factor (GCF).

Computing the GCF, we get

$$
\text{GCF}(4{x}^{2},320x,6\,000)=4
$$

Then, we rewrite each term in the original expression as a product with the $\text{GCF}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}-320x+6\,000 & = \\ 4\cdot ({x}^{2})+4\cdot (-80x)+4\cdot (1\,500)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the $\text{GCF}$ outside the parentheses and keep the remaining terms inside:

$$
\begin{aligned}4\cdot ({x}^{2})+4\cdot (-80x)+4\cdot (1\,500) & = \\ 4({x}^{2}-80x+1\,500)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the missing expression is ${x}^{2}-80x+1\,500.$

questions.knowledge_point: Factoring Trinomials With Positive Coefficients
questions.problem:
Find the minimum number of cakes the bakery needs to produce per week to make a weekly profit of $$6\,000.$

The bakery needs to produce$\,$
{{field-1}}$\,$ cakes per week.
questions.worked_solution:
From part 5, the required number of cakes $x$ is the solution to the equation

$$
4\cdot ({x}^{2}-80x+1\,500)=0.
$$

Dividing this equation by $4,$ we have

$$
{x}^{2}-80x+1\,500=0.
$$

To solve this equation, we want to find a factor pair of the constant term $(1\,500)$ that also adds up to the coefficient of the linear term $(-80).$ The required factors are $(-30)$ and $(-50).$

Using this factor pair, we write the linear term as $-80x=-30x-50x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-80x+1\,500 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-30x-50x+1\,500 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we factor the first two terms and the last two terms separately and then factor the expression completely:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-30x-50x+1\,500 & =0 \\ ({x}^{2}-30x)+(-50x+1\,500) & =0 \\ x(x-30)-50(x-30) & =0 \\ (x-30)(x-50)\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the solutions are $x=30$ or $x=50.$ Since we require the minimum solution, we conclude that the bakery needs to produce $30$ cakes per week to make a profit of $$6\,000.$

questions.knowledge_point: Converting a Recursive Formula to an Explicit Formula
questions.problem:
The bakery wants to increase its output by implementing a new production model. The number of cakes ${a}_{n}$ produced in the $n$th week since the implementation of the new model is given by the arithmetic sequence

$$
{a}_{n+1}={a}_{n}+4,\,{a}_{1}=19,\,n\ge 1
$$

What is the explicit formula for the $n$th term of this arithmetic sequence?

${a}_{n}=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
The explicit formula for the $n$th term of an arithmetic sequence is

$$
{a}_{n}={a}_{1}+(n-1)d,\,n\ge 1,
$$

so we need to determine the first term ${a}_{1}$ and the common difference $d.$

We are given that the first term is ${a}_{1}=19,$ and we can use the recursive rule to compute the second term as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} & ={a}_{1}+4 \\  & =19+4 \\  & =23\end{aligned}
$$

Using the first and second terms, we can compute the common difference:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & ={a}_{2}-{a}_{1} \\  & =23-19 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Now we substitute ${a}_{1}=19$ and $d=4$ into the formula for the $n$th term:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}+(n-1)d \\  & =19+(n-1)(4) \\  & =19+4n-4 \\  & =4n+15\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the formula for the $n$th term is

$$
{a}_{n}=4n+15,\,n\ge 1.
$$

$$

\begin{aligned}{a}_{2+2} & ={a}_{2+1}+{a}_{2} \\ {a}_{4} & ={a}_{3}+{a}_{2} \\ {a}_{4} & =-2+0 \\ {a}_{4} & =-2\end{aligned}

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Inverse of a Simple Rational Function
questions.problem: Find the inverse of the function $f(x)=\frac{3x+7}{5-x}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find ${f}^{-1}(x),$ we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y:$

$$
y=\frac{3x+7}{5-x}
$$

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives

$$
x=\frac{3y+7}{5-y}.
$$

Then, we make $y$ the subject of the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{3y+7}{5-y} \\ x(5-y) & =3y+7 \\ 5x-xy & =3y+7 \\ 5x-7 & =3y+xy \\ 5x-7 & =y(x+3) \\ y & =\frac{5x-7}{x+3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse function is 

$$
{f}^{-1}(x)=\frac{5x-7}{x+3}.
$$

questions.problem: The function $f(x)=\frac{k}{3x+5}$ has an inverse function given by ${f}^{-1}(x)=\frac{2-5x}{3x}.$ What is the value of $k?$
questions.worked_solution:
To find ${f}^{-1}(x),$ we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y:$

$$
y=\frac{k}{3x+5}
$$

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives

$$
x=\frac{k}{3y+5}.
$$

Then, we make $y$ the subject of the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{k}{3y+5} \\ x(3y+5) & =k \\ 3xy+5x & =k \\ 3xy & =k-5x \\ y & =\frac{k-5x}{3x}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse function is 

$$
{f}^{-1}(x)=\frac{k-5x}{3x}.
$$

Comparing our answer with the given expression, we conclude that $k=2.$

$$
\operatorname{cot}({270}^{∘})=\frac{\operatorname{cos}({270}^{∘})}{\operatorname{sin}({270}^{∘})}=\frac{0}{-1}=0.
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\operatorname{tan}({0}^{∘})+\operatorname{cot}({270}^{∘})=0+0=0.

questions.knowledge_point: Factoring a Polynomial With Leading Coefficients as a Difference of Squares
questions.problem: Factor $8{z}^{4}-128$ completely.
questions.worked_solution:
The difference of squares formula is given by

$$
{a}^{2}-{b}^{2}=(a+b)(a-b)
$$

Notice that all of the terms in our expression have a common factor of $8.$ To simplify the computation, we can factor out the $8,$ as follows:

$$
8{z}^{4}-128=8\cdot {z}^{4}-8\cdot 16=8({z}^{4}-16)
$$

The expression in parentheses can be written as a difference of squares:

$$
8({z}^{4}-16)=8({({z}^{2})}^{2}-{4}^{2})
$$

Now, we factor our expression using the difference of squares formula:

$$
8({({z}^{2})}^{2}-{4}^{2})=8({z}^{2}+4)({z}^{2}-4)
$$

Finally, we notice that the expression in the second set of parentheses is also a difference of squares. Therefore, the expression can be factored further, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}8({z}^{2}+4)({z}^{2}-4) & =8({z}^{2}+4)({z}^{2}-{2}^{2}) \\  & =8({z}^{2}+4)(z+2)(z-2)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the vertical asymptote of the function $f(x)={log}_{3}(4x+1).$
questions.worked_solution:
The equation of the vertical asymptote of the function $y={log}_{3}x$ is $x=0.$

To find the equation of the vertical asymptote of $f(x)$, we set the argument of the logarithmic term equal to zero, and solve for $x.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4x+1 & =0 \\ 4x & =-1 \\ x & =-\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the vertical asymptote is $x=-\frac{1}{4}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving a Quadratic Equation With Complex Roots by Completing the Square
questions.problem: What are the solutions of the equation $(x+3)^{2}=-4?$
questions.worked_solution:
The left-hand side is a perfect square. Therefore, we can solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+3)^{2} & =-4 \\ x+3 & =\pm \sqrt{-4} \\ x+3 & =\pm 2\,\text{i} \\ x & =-3\pm 2\,\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation has two solutions, $x=-3+2\,\text{i}$ and $x=-3-2\,\text{i}.$

questions.problem: Calculate $\int \frac{3}{2{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.$
questions.worked_solution:
We can just take the constant factor out of the integral, and then apply the power rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3}{2{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y & =\frac{3}{2}\int {y}^{-2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot (\frac{{y}^{(-2+1)}}{-2+1})+C \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot (\frac{{y}^{-1}}{-1})+C \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}\cdot {y}^{-1}+C \\  & =-\frac{3}{2y}+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Calculate $\int {e}^{2}\,\text{d}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
We can just take the constant factor out of the integral, and then apply the power rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {e}^{2}\,\text{d}x & ={e}^{2}\int 1\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{2}\int {x}^{0}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{2}\cdot \frac{{x}^{0+1}}{0+1}+C \\  & ={e}^{2}\cdot x+C \\  & ={e}^{2}x+C\end{aligned}
$$

In general, we can see that for any constant $k,$ we have $\int k\,\text{d}x=kx+C.$

questions.worked_solution:
Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if ${F}^{'}(x)=f(x),$ then integrating both sides of this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{'}(x) & =f(x) \\ \int {F}^{'}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We apply the power rule with $n=17$, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{17}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{17+1}}{17+1}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{18}}{18}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{18}}{18}+C) & = \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{18}}{18})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) & = \\ \frac{1}{18}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{18})+0 & = \\ \frac{1}{18}\cdot 18\,{x}^{17} & = \\ {x}^{17}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The multiplicity of the root $x=1$ in the polynomial $p(x)={x}^{3}-7{x}^{2}+14x-8$ is{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Since $x=1$ is a root of $p(x),$ the factor theorem tells us that $(x-1)$ is a factor of $p(x).$

Because $(x-1)$ is a factor of $p(x),$ we know that $(x-1)$ divides $p(x)$ with no remainder. So, to begin factoring $p(x),$ we can divide it by $(x-1)$ using synthetic division:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $1$ | $-7$ | $14$ | $-8$ |
|  | $↓$ | $1$ | $-6$ | $8$ |
|  | $1$ | $-6$ | $8$ | $0$ |

Therefore,

$$
\frac{p(x)}{x-1}={x}^{2}-6x+8,
$$

which means

$$
p(x)=(x-1)({x}^{2}-6x+8).
$$

We can factor the quadratic factor even further, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}p(x) & =(x-1)(x-2)(x-4).\end{aligned}
$$

The factor $(x-1)$ has an exponent of $1$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=1$ has multiplicity $1.$

- The factor $(x-1)$ has an exponent of $1$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=1$ has multiplicity $1.$

In conclusion, only the root $x=-1$ has multiplicity $2.$

If the figure above shows the graph of $f(x),$ then

${lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{(f(x)+2)^{4}}{(f(x)-5)^{3}}=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
Using the power and quotient rules, we can rewrite the given limit as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{(f(x)+2)^{4}}{(f(x)-5)^{3}} & =\frac{{({lim}_{x\to 0}(f(x)+2))}^{4}}{{({lim}_{x\to 0}(f(x)-5))}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

The above is true provided that  ${lim}_{x\to 0}f(x)$ exists.

We find from the graph that ${lim}_{x\to 0}f(x)=2.$ We calculate the limits of the numerator and denominator, separately.

$$
{lim}_{x\to 0}(f(x)+2)=2+2=4
$$

and

$$
{lim}_{x\to 0}(f(x)-5)=2-5=-3
$$

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{(f(x)+2)^{4}}{(f(x)-5)^{3}} & =\frac{{4}^{4}}{(-3)^{3}}=\frac{256}{-27}=-\frac{256}{27}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Find ${lim}_{x\to \,1}(3-x)^{3}(f(x)-4{x}^{2})^{5}$ for the function $f(x)$ plotted above.
questions.worked_solution:
From the graph, we get that ${lim}_{x\to \,1}f(x)=3.$ 

From the product rule, we have

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,1}(3-x)^{3}(f(x)-4{x}^{2})^{5}={lim}_{x\to \,1}(3-x)^{3}\cdot {lim}_{x\to \,1}(f(x)-4{x}^{2})^{5}.
$$

We calculate the limits of each factor, separately.

Applying the power rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,1}(3-x)^{3} & ={({lim}_{x\to \,1}(3-x))}^{3} \\  & =(3-1)^{3} \\  & ={2}^{3} \\  & =8,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,1}(f(x)-4{x}^{2})^{4} & ={({lim}_{x\to \,1}(f(x)-4{x}^{2}))}^{5} \\  & =(3-4(1)^{2})^{5} \\  & =(-1)^{5} \\  & =-1\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have
 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,1}(3-x)^{3}(f(x)-4{x}^{2})^{5} & ={lim}_{x\to \,1}(3-x)^{3}\cdot {lim}_{x\to \,1}(f(x)-4{x}^{2})^{5} \\  & =8\cdot (-1) \\  & =-8\,.\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving Equations Using Cross Multiplication
questions.problem: If $-\frac{10tx}{7}=\frac{5}{2},$ then $x=$
questions.worked_solution:
We need to isolate $x.$ To do this, we first cross-multiply:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{10tx}{7} & =\frac{5}{2} \\ \frac{-10tx}{7} & =\frac{5}{2} \\ 2\cdot (-10tx) & =7\cdot 5 \\ -20tx & =35\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we divide both sides of the equation by $-20t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-20tx & =35 \\ \frac{-20tx}{-20t} & =\frac{35}{-20t} \\ \frac{\cancel{-20t}x}{\cancel{-20t}} & =\frac{35}{-20t} \\ x & =-\frac{35}{20t}\end{aligned}
$$

We can further simplify the right-hand side as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-\frac{5\cdot 7}{5\cdot 4t} \\ x & =-\frac{\cancel{5}\cdot 7}{\cancel{5}\cdot 4t} \\ x & =-\frac{7}{4t}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Factoring a Trinomial With a Negative Quadratic Term
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can factor out a $(-4)$ from each of the terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}-4{y}^{2}+8y+12 & =-4({y}^{2}-2y-3)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we just need to factor the polynomial ${y}^{2}-2y-3$ in parentheses.

We start by listing the factor pairs of the constant term $(-3).$ The constant term is negative, so that means one of the factors is negative and the other is positive:

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & \times (-3) \\ (-1) & \times 3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find which factor pair adds up to the coefficient of the linear term $(-2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}1+(-3) & =-2 & ✓ \\ (-1)+3 & =2 & \times \end{aligned}
$$

Using the factor pair identified above, we write the linear term as $-2y=y-3y$ and then factor the expression completely:

$$
\begin{aligned}-4({y}^{2}-2y-3) & = \\ -4({y}^{2}+y-3y-3) & = \\ -4(({y}^{2}+y)+(-3y-3)) & = \\ -4(y(y+1)-3(y+1)) & = \\ -4(y-3)(y+1)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Relating a Derivative to a Rate of Change
questions.problem:
To measure the success of an amusement park, Ed uses the following three functions that model the daily number of visitors to the park $t$ minutes after the park is opened to the public.

- $N(t)$ - the number of people inside the park

- $E(t)$ - the rate at which people enter the park

- $L(t)$ - the rate at which people leave the park

What is the relationship between the functions above?
questions.worked_solution:
The function $N(t)$ gives the number of people inside the park $t$ minutes after opening. Then,

$$
{N}^{'}(t)=\frac{\text{d}N(t)}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{Change in }N}{\text{Change in }t}.
$$

Thus, ${N}^{'}(t)$ gives the rate at which the number of people inside the park changes $t$ minutes after opening.

In addition, we can compute the rate of change of the number of people inside the park at time $t$ by finding the difference between the entry and exit rates at time $t.$ That is,

$$
{N}^{'}(t)=E(t)-L(t).
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Unit Vector Parallel to a Given Vector
questions.problem: Let $b=[\begin{aligned}8 \\ -6\end{aligned}].$ Find a unit vector that is parallel to $b$ and points the same direction.
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that to find a unit vector that is parallel to a given vector, we need to divide the given vector by its length:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =\frac{b}{|\,b\,|}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula for the magnitude of a vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|\,b\,| & =\sqrt{{8}^{2}+(-6)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{64+36} \\  & =\sqrt{100} \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we divide $b$ by its length and get the following unit vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =\frac{b}{|b|} \\  & =\frac{1}{10}\cdot b \\  & =\frac{1}{10}\cdot [\begin{aligned}8 \\ -6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5} \\ -\frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Inverse of a Simple Rational Function
questions.problem: Find the inverse of the function $f(x)=\frac{6-5x}{x+7}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find ${f}^{-1}(x),$ we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y:$

$$
y=\frac{6-5x}{x+7}
$$

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives

$$
x=\frac{6-5y}{y+7}.
$$

Then, we make $y$ the subject of the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{6-5y}{y+7} \\ x(y+7) & =6-5y \\ xy+7x & =6-5y \\ xy+5y & =6-7x \\ y(x+5) & =6-7x \\ y & =\frac{6-7x}{x+5}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse function is 

$$
{f}^{-1}(x)=\frac{6-7x}{x+5}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Factoring a Quartic Polynomial With Only Two Real Factors
questions.problem:
Find the polynomial $P(x)$ given that 

$$
2{x}^{4}-10{x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+6x-5=(x-5)(x+1)P(x).
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)=2{x}^{4}-10{x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+6x-5.$ We know that $(x+1)$ and $(x-5)$ are factors of $f(x),$ and we need to find its other factors.

Because $(x+1)$ is a factor of $f(x),$ we know that $(x+1)$ divides $f(x)$ with no remainder. So, to begin factoring $f(x),$ we can divide it by $(x+1)$ using synthetic division:

|  | ${x}^{4}$ | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $-1$ | $2$ | $-10$ | $-1$ | $6$ | $-5$ |
|  | $↓$ | $-2$ | $12$ | $-11$ | $5$ |
|  | $2$ | $-12$ | $11$ | $-5$ | $0$ |

Therefore,

$$
\frac{2{x}^{4}-10{x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+6x-5}{x+1}=2{x}^{3}-12{x}^{2}+11x-5,
$$

which means that

$$
2{x}^{4}-10{x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+6x-5=(x+1)(2{x}^{3}-12{x}^{2}+11x-5).
$$

Now, because $(x-5)$ is also a factor of $f(x),$ it must be a factor of the quotient $(2{x}^{3}-12{x}^{2}+11x-5).$ So, we divide this quotient by $(x-5)$ using synthetic division once more:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $5$ | $2$ | $-12$ | $11$ | $-5$ |
|  | $↓$ | $10$ | $-10$ | $5$ |
|  | $2$ | $-2$ | $1$ | $0$ |

Therefore,

$$
\frac{2{x}^{3}-12{x}^{2}+11x-5}{x-5}=2{x}^{2}-2x+1,
$$

which means that

$$
2{x}^{4}-10{x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+6x-5=(x-5)(x+1)(2{x}^{2}-2x+1).
$$

To see whether the quadratic polynomial $2{x}^{2}-2x+1$ can be factored any further, we calculate its discriminant:

$$
{b}^{2}-4ac=(-2)^{2}-4(2)(1)=-4<0
$$

So, the quadratic polynomial $2{x}^{2}-2x+1$ cannot be factored over the real numbers since its discriminant is negative. 

Therefore, the full factorization of $f(x)$ over the real numbers is given by 

$$
2{x}^{4}-10{x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+6x-5=(x-5)(x+1){{(2{x}^{2}-2x+1)}_{⏟}}_{P(x)}.
$$

Finally, $P(x)=2{x}^{2}-2x+1.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Index of a Term Given the Recursive Formula
questions.problem:
What is the index of the term $192$ for the geometric sequence below?

$$
f(n+1)=2f(n),\,f(1)=3,\,n\ge 1
$$
questions.worked_solution:
This geometric sequence is given as a recurrence relation, i.e.,

$$
f(n+1)=r\cdot f(n).
$$

Therefore:

$$
f(1)=3,\,r=2.
$$

We're interested in finding $n$ such that $f(n)=192.$ Using the formula for the $n$th term, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(n) & =f(1)\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\ 192 & =3\cdot {2}^{n-1} \\ \frac{192}{3} & ={2}^{n-1} \\ 64 & ={2}^{n-1} \\ {2}^{6} & ={2}^{n-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the exponents gives:

$$
6=n-1\,⟹\,n=7
$$

Therefore, $192$ is the $7$th term of the sequence.

questions.knowledge_point: Rearranging and Solving a Quadratic Equation With Complex Roots
questions.problem: Solve  the equation $\,-8x+12=-2{x}^{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write the equation in standard form by bringing all of the terms to the left-hand side. This gives the equation

$$
2{x}^{2}-8x+12=0.
$$

We can find the roots of a quadratic equation using the quadratic formula:

$$
x=\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a}
$$

In this case, the coefficients are $a=2,b=-8,$ and $c=12.$ Substituting these values into the quadratic formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{-(-8)\pm \sqrt{(-8)^{2}-4(2)(12)}}{2(2)} \\  & =\frac{8\pm \sqrt{64-96}}{4} \\  & =\frac{8\pm \sqrt{-32}}{4} \\  & =\frac{8\pm 4\sqrt{-2}}{4} \\  & =\frac{8\pm 4\sqrt{2}\,\text{i}}{4} \\  & =2\pm \sqrt{2}\,\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation has two solutions, $x=2+\sqrt{2}\,\text{i}$ and $x=2-\sqrt{2}\,\text{i}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving Logarithmic Equations Containing Nonlinear Arguments
questions.problem: Solve the equation ${log}_{4}({x}^{2}+4)={log}_{4}(-3x+2).$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the logarithms on both sides of the equation have the same base, we can equate the arguments. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{4}({x}^{2}+4) & ={log}_{4}(-3x+2) \\ {x}^{2}+4 & =-3x+2 \\ {x}^{2}+3x+2 & =0 \\ (x+2)(x+1) & =0 \\ x & =-2,-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's now check for extraneous solutions by substituting back into the original equation:

- Substituting $x=-2$ back into the original equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{4}({x}^{2}+4) & \overset{?}{=}{log}_{4}(-3x+2) \\ {log}_{4}((-2)^{2}+4) & \overset{?}{=}{log}_{4}(-3(-2)+2) \\ {log}_{4}(8) & ={log}_{4}(8).\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=-2$ is a valid solution.

- Substituting $x=-1$ back into the original equation, we get

$$

questions.knowledge_point: Expressing the Tangent of a Negative Angle in Terms of a Reference Angle
questions.problem: What is $\operatorname{tan}(-\frac{17\pi }{12})$ expressed in terms of a reference angle?
questions.worked_solution:
We wish to express $\operatorname{tan}(-\frac{17\pi }{12})$ in terms of $\operatorname{tan}{\theta }_{R},$ where ${\theta }_{R}$ is the reference angle corresponding to the angle $\theta =-\frac{17\pi }{12}.$ 

To express $\operatorname{tan}(-\frac{17\pi }{12})$ in terms of $\operatorname{tan}{\theta }_{R},$ we proceed as follows: 

- **Step 1**: Find the corresponding coterminal angle that lies in the range $[0,2\pi ).$ We do this by adding integer multiples of $2\pi $ until we get our desired angle:

$$
-\frac{17\pi }{12}+2\pi =\frac{7\pi }{12}\,✓
$$

Therefore,

$$
\operatorname{tan}(-\frac{17\pi }{12})=\operatorname{tan}(\frac{7\pi }{12}).
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/history-question-import-2026-10-04/import-ready/assets/7828b40e3fba874611bb9c20e38e0880375aec389ae8ec646d92ea1e1b276883.png)

- **Step 2**: Compute the reference angle. Since $\theta =\frac{7\pi }{12}$ is in the $2$nd quadrant, the reference angle is

$$
{\theta }_{R}=\pi -\frac{7\pi }{12}=\frac{5\pi }{12}.
$$

- **Step 3**: Determine the correct sign. The tangent function is negative $(-)$ in the second quadrant. Therefore,

$$
\operatorname{tan}(-\frac{17\pi }{12})=-\operatorname{tan}{\theta }_{R}=-\operatorname{tan}(\frac{5\pi }{12})
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\operatorname{tan}(-\frac{17\pi }{12})=-\operatorname{tan}(\frac{5\pi }{12}).
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Measure of an Obtuse Angle in a Triangle Using the Law of Sines
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/history-question-import-2026-10-04/import-ready/assets/1d60d9f28a5456d0814164572315767d733fa111de88aebd51116a6f7f3e8580.png)

Calculate, to the nearest tenth, the measure of the obtuse angle $X.$
questions.worked_solution:
The Law of Sines states that

$$
\frac{\operatorname{sin}X}{x}=\frac{\operatorname{sin}Y}{y}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
x=16,\,m∠Y={36}^{∘},\,y=14,
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{sin}X}{16} & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}{36}^{∘}}{14} \\ \operatorname{sin}X & =16\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}{36}^{∘}}{14} \\  & =\frac{8\cdot \operatorname{sin}{36}^{∘}}{7} \\  & \approx \frac{8\cdot 0.587\,8}{7} \\  & \approx 0.671\,8,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $4$ decimal places. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠X & \approx \operatorname{arcsin}(0.671\,8)\approx {42.2}^{∘},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to the nearest tenth. But this is less than ${90}^{∘}.$ To get the true value of $X,$ we subtract our answer from ${180}^{∘}:$

$$
m∠X\approx {180}^{∘}-{42.20}^{∘}\approx {137.8}^{∘},
$$

rounded to the nearest tenth.

questions.knowledge_point: Cases Reducing to Solving a Quadratic by Factoring
questions.problem: Given that $-2{x}^{2}-4kx-8k=0,$ where $k$ is a **positive** constant, has exactly one real solution, what is the value of $k?$
questions.worked_solution:
A quadratic equation has exactly one real root if the discriminant is equal to zero: $D=0.$

The coefficients of our quadratic equation are the following:

$$
a=-2,\,b=-4k,\,c=-8k
$$

So, computing the discriminant, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}D & ={b}^{2}-4ac \\  & =(-4k)^{2}-4(-2)(-8k) \\  & =16{k}^{2}-64k.\end{aligned}
$$

To have exactly one real solution, we need $D=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}16{k}^{2}-64k & =0 \\ 16k(k-4) & =0 \\ k & =0,4\end{aligned}
$$

Since $k$ must be positive, we conclude that $k=4.$

questions.knowledge_point: Estimating a Variance or Standard Deviation
questions.problem:
Consider the frequency table below for a continuous variable $x.$ Assuming that the observations within each class interval are uniformly distributed, the total number of observations is $n=20,$ and the estimated sample mean is $\overset{―}{x}\approx 13.5.$

| Range | Frequency $({f}_{i})$ |
| --- | --- |
| $0\le x<10$ | $8$ |
| $10\le x<20$ | $7$ |
| $20\le x<30$ | $5$ |

$$

$$

Based on these distributional assumptions, find the standard estimate for the sample standard deviation ${\sigma }_{n}.$

Rounded to one decimal place, ${\sigma }_{n}\approx $
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
Given a frequency table containing continuous data split into $K$ classes, the variance can be estimated as follows:

$$
{\sigma }_{n}^{2}\approx \frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{K}{f}_{i}\cdot ({m}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2},
$$

where

- ${f}_{i}$ is the frequency of the $i$th class,

- ${m}_{i}$ is the midpoint of the $i$th class,

- $n$ is the total number of observations, and

- $\overset{―}{x}$ is the mean.

To find the variance, we add columns to our table for the midpoints of each interval, the squared deviations of the midpoints from the mean, and the products of the squared deviations and frequencies.

| Range | ${f}_{i}$ | ${m}_{i}$ | ${({m}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})}^{2}$ | ${f}_{i}{({m}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})}^{2}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0\le x<10$ | $8$ | $5$ | $72.25$ | $578$ |
| $10\le x<20$ | $7$ | $15$ | $2.25$ | $15.75$ |
| $20\le x<30$ | $5$ | $25$ | $132.25$ | $661.25$ |

$$

$$

Then, we divide the sum of all the values in the last column by $20$ (the total number of observations):

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{n}^{2} & \approx \frac{578+15.75+661.25}{20} \\  & =\frac{1255}{20} \\  & =62.75\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the standard deviation is the square root of the variance:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{n} & =\sqrt{62.75}\approx 7.9\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Applying Several Transformations: Horizontal Stretch Followed By Horizontal Shift Inside Parentheses
questions.problem:
Given the graph of $y=f(x),$ we apply the following transformations in the order given:

- Stretch it by a scale factor of $8$ parallel to the $y$-axis

- Stretch it by a scale factor of $5$ parallel to the $x$-axis

- Translate it to the left by $10$ units

What is the final function expression after applying all the transformations?
questions.worked_solution:
To find the expression, let's apply each of the transformations in turn.

- Stretching the graph of $y=f(x)$ by a scale factor of $8$ parallel to the $y$-axis is equivalent to multiplying the function expression by $8.$ Applying this transformation, we obtain 

$$
y=8f(x).
$$

- Stretching the graph of $y=8f(x)$ by a scale factor of $5$ parallel to the $x$-axis is equivalent to replacing every instance of $x$ with $\frac{1}{5}x.$ Applying this transformation, we obtain 

$$
y=8f(\frac{1}{5}x)=8f(\frac{x}{5}).
$$

- Translating the graph of $y=8f(\frac{x}{5})$ by $10$ units to the left is equivalent to replacing every instance of $x$ with $(x+10).$ Applying this transformation, we obtain 

$$
y=8f(\frac{1}{5}(x+10))=8f(\frac{x}{5}+2).
$$

Therefore, the final function expression is $y=8f(\frac{x}{5}+2).$

questions.worked_solution:
The recursive formula is

$$
{a}_{n+2}={a}_{n+1}+{a}_{n}.

Substituting $n=1$ into the recursive formula gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1+2} & ={a}_{1+1}+{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{3} & ={a}_{2}+{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{3} & =6+1 \\ {a}_{3} & =7\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $n=2$ into the recursive formula gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{2+2} & ={a}_{2+1}+{a}_{2} \\ {a}_{4} & ={a}_{3}+{a}_{2} \\ {a}_{4} & =7+6 \\ {a}_{4} & =13\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${a}_{4}=13.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Distance Between a Point and a Line
questions.problem: Find the shortest distance between the point $(2,5)$ and the line $3y+2x=6.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rewrite the equation of the given line in slope-intercept form:

$$
\begin{aligned}3y+2x & =6 \\ 3y & =-2x+6 \\ y & =-\frac{2}{3}x+2\end{aligned}
$$

Let's draw a diagram describing our situation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/history-question-import-2026-10-04/import-ready/assets/2e9224ad718acaea23e8e1b50ac0f4c30099710652db7528406ec9ec11baaecd.png)

Next, we find the equation of the line that's perpendicular to $y=-\frac{2}{3}x+2$ and passes through the point $(2,5).$

 The given line has a slope of $-\frac{2}{3},$ so our perpendicular line must have a slope of $\frac{3}{2}.$

Using point-slope form and simplifying, we obtain the equation of the perpendicular line:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-5 & =\frac{3}{2}(x-2) \\ y-5 & =\frac{3}{2}x-3 \\ y & =\frac{3}{2}x+2\end{aligned}
$$

We now find the point where the two lines intersect. To do this, we solve the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}y=-\frac{2}{3}x+2 \\ y=\frac{3}{2}x+2\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this system by putting the two equations equal to one another and solving for $x.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{3}x+2 & =\frac{3}{2}x+2 \\ -\frac{2}{3}x-\frac{3}{2}x & =2-2 \\ -\frac{13}{6}x & =0 \\ x & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=0$ into either of the two equations gives $y=2.$ So, our solution is $x=0$ and $y=2.$ So, the lines intersect at the point $(0,2).$

Finally, we find the distance $d$ between the points $(2,5)$ and $(0,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\sqrt{({x}_{2}-{x}_{1})^{2}+({y}_{2}-{y}_{1})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(0-2)}^{2}+(2-5)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4+9} \\  & =\sqrt{13}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the shortest distance between the point $(2,5)$ and the line $3y+2x=6$ is $\sqrt{13}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Factoring a Polynomial With Multiple Variables as a Difference of Squares
questions.problem: Factor the expression $81{m}^{4}-{n}^{4}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The difference of squares formula is given by

$$
{a}^{2}-{b}^{2}=(a+b)(a-b)
$$

Notice that our expression can be written as a difference of squares:

$$
81{m}^{4}-{n}^{4}={(9{m}^{2})}^{2}-{({n}^{2})}^{2}
$$

Now, we factor our expression using the difference of squares formula:

$$
{(9{m}^{2})}^{2}-{({n}^{2})}^{2}=(9{m}^{2}+{n}^{2})(9{m}^{2}-{n}^{2})
$$

Finally, we notice that the expression in the second set of parentheses is also a difference of squares: 

$$
9{m}^{2}-{n}^{2}={(3m)}^{2}-{n}^{2}
$$

Therefore, the expression can be factored further, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(9{m}^{2}+{n}^{2})(9{m}^{2}-{n}^{2}) & =(9{m}^{2}+{n}^{2})(3m+n)(3m-n)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding Exact Solutions of Exponential Equations
questions.problem: Expressed in terms of ${log}_{9},$ what value of $y$ satisfies the equation ${9}^{2y+1}={5}^{-y}?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we take ${log}_{9}$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{9}^{2y+1} & ={5}^{-y} \\ {log}_{9}({9}^{2y+1}) & ={log}_{9}({5}^{-y})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that ${log}_{b}({b}^{c})=c$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

$$
2y+1={log}_{9}({5}^{-y})
$$

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
2y+1=-y{log}_{9}(5)
$$

Finally, we solve for $y,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2y+1 & =-y{log}_{9}(5) \\ 2y+y{log}_{9}(5) & =-1 \\ y(2+{log}_{9}(5)) & =-1 \\ y & =-\frac{1}{2+{log}_{9}(5)}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find $|z|$ if $z=2-3\text{i}.$
questions.worked_solution:
For a complex number $z=a+b\text{i},$ the magnitude of $z$ is given by

$$
|z|=\sqrt{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}.
$$

For the complex number $z=2-3\text{i},$ we have $a=2$ and $b=-3.$ So, the magnitude is given by

$$

$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Similarity Transformations
questions.problem:
Which of the following transformations map any polygon to a similar polygon?

I. - Stretching with a stretch factor of $2$ in the $x$-direction and a stretch factor of $4$ in the $y$-direction
II. - Translation by $3$ units to the left and $4$ units upward
III. - Dilation of scale factor $2$ with center $O,$ then reflection across the $y$-axis
questions.worked_solution:
A similarity transformation is any transformation made up of rigid motions (rotations, reflections, and translations) and dilations.

A similarity transformation will map any polygon to a similar polygon.

With that in mind, let's examine each of the transformations in turn.

- Transformation I includes stretching with different factors in the $x$- and $y$-direction. Thus, it is not a similarity transformation.

- Transformation II is a combination of two translations, which are rigid motions. Thus, it is a similarity transformation.

- Transformation III is a combination of dilation of scale factor $2$ and a reflection. Thus, it is a similarity transformation.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

questions.knowledge_point: Computing an Inverse Function Using the Definition
questions.problem: Suppose that $f(x)=2x+6$ and $g(x)=\frac{x}{2}+k.$ If $g$ is the inverse of $f,$ then $k=$
questions.worked_solution:
If $g$ is the inverse of $f,$ then we must have:

$$
g(f(x))=x
$$

To find $g(f(x)),$ we write down the function $g$ and replace every occurrence of $x$ with $f(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(x) & =\frac{x}{2}+k \\ g(f(x)) & =\frac{f(x)}{2}+k\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $f(x)=2x+6$ into the right-hand side of our expression and simplify, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}g(f(x)) & =\frac{f(x)}{2}+k \\  & =\frac{2x+6}{2}+k \\  & =x+3+k\end{aligned}
$$

However, we also know that $g(f(x))=x.$ Equating the expression above with $x$ and solving for $k$ gives:

$$

questions.knowledge_point: Classifying Even and Odd Functions Using the Algebraic Definition
questions.problem: Is the function $f(x)=2{x}^{3}-2x$ even, odd, or neither?
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that

- a function is even if $f(-x)=f(x)$ for all $x$

- a function is odd if $f(-x)=-f(x)$ for all $x$

Computing $f(-x)$ for the given function and comparing it to $f(x),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =2(-x)^{3}-2(-x) \\  & =-2{x}^{3}+2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(-x)\ne f(x),$ the function is not even.

Lastly, we compute $-f(x)$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}-f(x) & =-(2{x}^{3}-2x) \\  & =-2{x}^{3}+2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(-x)=-f(x),$ the function is odd.

questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Index of a Term Given Two Terms
questions.problem:
Given an arithmetic sequence that has ${a}_{4}=13$ and ${a}_{8}=41,$ what is the index of the term $90?$

Answer: {{answer}}
questions.worked_solution:
To construct the formula for the sequence, we need to know the common difference $d$ and the first term ${a}_{1}.$

Since we are given ${a}_{4}=13$ and ${a}_{8}=41,$ we can find the common difference by dividing the total difference by the number of jumps:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\frac{{a}_{8}-{a}_{4}}{8-4} \\  & =\frac{41-13}{8-4} \\  & =\frac{28}{4} \\  & =7\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since ${a}_{4}=13$ is $3$ jumps after ${a}_{1},$ we can determine the first term of the sequence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{4} & ={a}_{1}+3d \\ 13 & ={a}_{1}+3(7) \\ 13 & ={a}_{1}+21 \\ -8 & ={a}_{1}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the formula for the $n$th term is:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}+(n-1)d \\  & =-8+(n-1)(7) \\  & =-8+7n-7 \\  & =7n-15\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for the value of $n$ that gives ${a}_{n}=90,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =7n-15 \\ 90 & =7n-15 \\ 105 & =7n \\ \frac{105}{7} & =n \\ 15 & =n\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $90$ is the $15$th term of the sequence.

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Common Ratio Given Some Additional Information About the Geometric Sequence
questions.problem:
The third term of a geometric sequence is $108$ and its fifth term is $3.$  Find the common ratio $r$ of this sequence given that $r$ is positive.

Answer: {{answer}}
questions.worked_solution:
To find the common ratio $r$ of a geometric sequence given two terms ${a}_{m}$ and ${a}_{n},$ we use the formula

$$
{r}^{n-m}=\frac{{a}_{n}}{{a}_{m}}.
$$

In this case, we're given ${a}_{5}=3$ and ${a}_{3}=108.$ Substituting $n=5$ and $m=3$ into the formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{5-3} & =\frac{{a}_{5}}{{a}_{3}} \\ {r}^{2} & =\frac{3}{108} \\ {r}^{2} & =\frac{1}{36}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, solving the equation for $r$ and considering that $r$ is positive, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{2} & =\frac{1}{36} \\ {r}^{2} & ={(\frac{1}{6})}^{2} \\ r & =\frac{1}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Writing the Equation of a Parabola With Leading Coefficients in Vertex Form
questions.problem:
The curve $y=4{x}^{2}-24x+24$ can be written as $y=a(x+b)^{2}+c.$ Calculate $a+b+c.$

Answer: {{answer}}
questions.worked_solution:
To express the equation of the parabola in vertex form, we need to complete the square. 

First, we take out a factor of $4$ from the entire expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}-24x+24 & =4({x}^{2}-6x+6)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we complete the square for the expression inside the parentheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-6x+6 & = \\ {x}^{2}-2\cdot 3\cdot x+6 & = \\ {x}^{2}-2\cdot 3\cdot x+{3}^{2}-{3}^{2}+6 & = \\ ({x}^{2}-2\cdot 3\cdot x+{3}^{2})-{3}^{2}+6 & = \\ (x-3)^{2}-{3}^{2}+6 & = \\ (x-3)^{2}-9+6 & = \\ (x-3)^{2}-3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute this result back into our original expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}4({x}^{2}-6x+6) & = \\ 4((x-3)^{2}-3) & = \\ 4(x-3)^{2}-12\end{aligned}
$$

So,  $a+b+c=4+(-3)+(-12)=-11.$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying True Statements About Operations on Polynomials
questions.problem:
If $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ are polynomials of degree $3$ and $7,$ respectively, which of the following statements are true?

I. - $P+Q$ is always a polynomial of degree $10$
II. - $P-Q$ is always a polynomial of degree $4$
III. - $P\cdot Q$ is always a polynomial of degree $10$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's look at each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. For example, suppose $P(x)={x}^{3}$ and $Q(x)={x}^{7}.$ Then $P+Q={x}^{3}+{x}^{7},$ which is not a polynomial of degree $10.$

- Statement II is false. For example, suppose $P(x)={x}^{3}$ and $Q(x)={x}^{7}.$ Then $P-Q={x}^{3}-{x}^{7},$ which is not a polynomial of degree $4.$

- Statement III is true. The highest-degree terms in $P$ and $Q$ must contain ${x}^{3}$ and ${x}^{7},$ respectively. Therefore, the highest-degree term in $P\cdot Q$ must contain ${x}^{3}\cdot {x}^{7}={x}^{3+7}={x}^{10},$ meaning that $P\cdot Q$ has degree $10.$

In conclusion, only statement III is true.

questions.worked_solution:
We can form a triangle by creating a vertical line from $A$ to the $x$-axis. Let us call ${\theta }^{'}$ the angle that is formed with the $x$-axis such that ${\theta }^{'}+\theta =2\pi $

Using the tangent ratio, we have

$$
\operatorname{tan}{\theta }^{'}=\frac{6}{2\sqrt{3}}=\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}}=\sqrt{3}.
$$

Finally, using the inverse tangent, we get

$$
{\theta }^{'}=\operatorname{arctan}\sqrt{3}=\frac{\pi }{3}.
$$

Finally, using $\theta +{\theta }^{'}=2\pi ,$ we get $\theta =2\pi -\frac{\pi }{3}=\frac{5\pi }{3}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying the Intervals on Which a Function is Invertible Given a Description
questions.problem:
Given that $f(x)=|x-4|+2,$ on which of the following intervals is $f(x)$ invertible?

I. - $x\in (-\infty ,3)$
II. - $x\in (1,\infty )$
III. - $x\in (-\infty ,5]$
questions.worked_solution:
The graph of the function $f(x)=|x-4|+2$ can be obtained in the following way:

- Take the curve $y=|x|.$

- Translate it by $4$ units to the right,  to get $y=|x-4|.$

- Finally, translate $y=|x-4|$ by $2$ units up to get $f(x)=|x-4|+2.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/history-question-import-2026-10-04/import-ready/assets/56956d0f23ae6828098507712fd00525dc4f114a195716dc16e63d8475e9c143.png)

A function is invertible on a particular interval if and only if it's a one-to-one function on that interval. To determine the intervals on which the function is invertible, we use the horizontal line test. 

- The function $f(x)$ is invertible on the interval $x\in (-\infty ,3).$  Indeed, on this interval, any horizontal line will intersect the curve at most once, no matter where we draw the line.

- The function $f(x)$ is not invertible on any of the intervals $x\in (1,\infty )$  and $(-\infty ,5].$ On each of these intervals, some horizontal lines will intersect the curve more than once.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only".

questions.worked_solution:
The horizontal asymptote of the curve $y=k{(\frac{1}{2})}^{x}+c$ is $y=c.$ In the graph above, the horizontal asymptote is $y=-3.$ Hence, $c=-3.$

We can solve for $k$ by finding a point on the graph and substituting for $x$ and $y.$ The labeled point on the graph is $(0,1),$ so we substitute $x=0$ and $y=1$ into the function and solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}k{(\frac{1}{2})}^{x}+c & =y \\ k{(\frac{1}{2})}^{x}-3 & =y \\ k{(\frac{1}{2})}^{0}-3 & =1 \\ k-3 & =1 \\ k & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
k-c=4-(-3)=7.
$$

The equation of the curve is $y=4{(\frac{1}{2})}^{x}-3.$

questions.problem: Find the root of $f(x)=3\sqrt[6]{3x+13}-6.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the root of $f(x),$  we must solve $f(x)=0:$

$$
3\sqrt[6]{3x+13}-6=0
$$

We solve this equation by making $x$ the subject, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3\sqrt[6]{3x+13}-6 & =0 \\ 3\sqrt[6]{3x+13} & =6 \\ \sqrt[6]{3x+13} & =2 \\ (\sqrt[6]{3x+13})^{6} & ={2}^{6} \\ 3x+13 & =64 \\ 3x & =51 \\ x & =17\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we must check the answer by substituting it back into the initial equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}3\sqrt[6]{3\cdot 17+13}-6 & =0 \\ 3\sqrt[6]{64}-6 & =0 \\ 3\cdot 2-6 & =0 \\ 0 & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the root of $f(x)$ is $x=17.$

questions.problem: What is the diameter of a circle if its area is $\frac{9}{25}\pi ?$
questions.worked_solution:
The formula for the area of a circle is $A=\pi {r}^{2}$, where $r$ is the radius. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\pi {r}^{2} \\ \frac{9}{25}\pi  & =\pi {r}^{2} \\ \frac{9}{25}\cancel{\pi } & =\cancel{\pi }{r}^{2} \\ r & =\sqrt{\frac{9}{25}} \\ r & =\frac{3}{5}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the diameter is

$$
d=2\cdot r=2\cdot \frac{3}{5}=\frac{6}{5}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Maps Presented in Function Notation That Are Rigid Motions
questions.problem:
Which of the following transformations map every polygon to a congruent polygon?

I. - $(x,y)↦(x-1,y)$
II. - $(x,y)↦(-y,x)$
III. - $(x,y)↦(2x,y)$
questions.worked_solution:
A rigid motion is a transformation that preserves distances. There are three types of rigid motions:

- Translations

- Rotations

- Reflections

Also, two polygons are congruent if and only if one can be mapped to another using a combination of rigid motions.

With that in mind, let's examine each of the transformations in turn.

- Transformation I is a translation of $1$ unit to the right. This is a rigid motion. So, it maps every polygon to a congruent polygon.

- Transformation II is a rotation of ${90}^{∘}$ counterclockwise about the origin. This is a rigid motion. So, it maps every polygon to a congruent polygon.

- Transformation III is a stretch with a stretch factor of $2$ in the $x$-direction. This is *not* a rigid motion. So, it does not map every polygon to a congruent polygon.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

questions.knowledge_point: Expressing a Reciprocal Trigonometric Ratio in Terms of a Reference Angle
questions.problem: Express $\operatorname{cot}(\frac{7\pi }{10})$ in terms of a reference angle.
questions.worked_solution:
To help us to visualize the angle, we first convert the measure of the angle into degrees. 

To convert the measure of an angle in radians to an equivalent measure in degrees, we multiply the measure in radians by $\frac{{180}^{∘}}{\pi }.$ This gives

$$
(\frac{7\pi }{10})\cdot (\frac{{180}^{∘}}{\pi })={126}^{∘}.
$$

Therefore $\frac{7\pi }{10}$ is equivalent to ${126}^{∘},$ which lies in the $2\text{nd}$ quadrant.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/history-question-import-2026-10-04/import-ready/assets/89b5e2656378adb5d91c9f58c261e4beaae252b67819b904bf209f6ed8a5a25e.png)

To express $\operatorname{cot}(\frac{7\pi }{10})$ in terms of $\operatorname{cot}{\theta }_{R},$ we follow three steps:

- Find its reference angle ${\theta }_{R}.$

- Calculate the value of the function for ${\theta }_{R}.$

- Determine whether the resulting value is positive or negative.

**Step 1**: Since $\theta =\frac{7\pi }{10}$ is in the $2$nd quadrant, the reference angle ${\theta }_{R}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{R} & =\pi -\theta  \\  & =\pi -\frac{7\pi }{10} \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: The given ratio is $\operatorname{cot}(\frac{7\pi }{10})$, and therefore we're interested in $\operatorname{cot}{\theta }_{R}=\operatorname{cot}(\frac{3\pi }{10}).$

**Step 3:** The ratio $\operatorname{cot}(\frac{7\pi }{10})$ must be negative because tangent (and therefore cotangent) is always negative in the $2$nd quadrant. Therefore,

$$
\operatorname{cot}(\frac{7\pi }{10})=-\operatorname{cot}(\frac{3\pi }{10}).
$$

questions.problem: Given that $m\ge 0$ is an integer, simplify $\frac{m(m+1)!}{(m+2)!}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice the following:

$$
(m+2)!=(m+2)\cdot (m+1)!
$$

Then, we cancel the $(m+1)!$ that occurs in both the numerator and the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{m(m+1)!}{(m+2)!} & =\frac{m\cdot (m+1)!}{(m+2)\cdot (m+1)!} \\  & =\frac{m\cdot \cancel{(m+1)!}}{(m+2)\cdot \cancel{(m+1)!}} \\  & =\frac{m}{m+2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing a Reciprocal Ratio of a Quadrantal Angle
questions.problem:
Find the value of $\operatorname{sec}0+\operatorname{csc}(\frac{\pi }{2}).$

Answer: {{answer}}
questions.worked_solution:
The angles $0$ and $\frac{\pi }{2}$ are quadrantal angles. Let's draw out the quadrantal angles on the unit circle.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/history-question-import-2026-10-04/import-ready/assets/792a778286533d589a3410223aaf197b07e64ea77566042d7bb8ac13fbad9768.png)

- Let's first consider the angle $0.$ From the unit circle, we see that the angle $0$ corresponds to the point $(1,0).$  Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the $x$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{cos}0=1.$ Therefore, using the fact that $\operatorname{sec}\theta =\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}\theta },$ we have

$$
\operatorname{sec}0=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}0}=\frac{1}{1}=1.
$$

- Now, let's consider the angle $\frac{\pi }{2}.$ From the unit circle, we see that the angle $\frac{\pi }{2}$ corresponds to the point $(0,1).$  Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the $y$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{2})=1.$ Therefore, using the fact that $\operatorname{csc}\theta =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}\theta },$ we have

$$
\operatorname{csc}(\frac{\pi }{2})=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{2})}=\frac{1}{1}=1.
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\operatorname{sec}0+\operatorname{csc}(\frac{\pi }{2})=1+1=2.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Multiplicity of a Root of a Cubic Polynomial Using Synthetic Division
questions.problem: What is the multiplicity of the root $x=4$ in the polynomial $p(x)={x}^{3}-6{x}^{2}+32?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $x=4$ is a root of $p(x),$ the factor theorem tells us that $(x-4)$ is a factor of $p(x).$

Because $(x-4)$ is a factor of $p(x),$ we know that $(x-4)$ divides $p(x)$ with no remainder. So, to begin factoring $p(x),$ we can divide it by $(x-4)$ using synthetic division:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $4$ | $1$ | $-6$ | $0$ | $32$ |
|  | $↓$ | $4$ | $-8$ | $-32$ |
|  | $1$ | $-2$ | $-8$ | $0$ |

Therefore,

$$
\frac{p(x)}{x-4}={x}^{2}-2x-8,
$$

which means that

$$
p(x)=(x-4)({x}^{2}-2x-8).
$$

We can factor the quadratic factor even further, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}p(x) & =(x-4)(x+2)(x-4) \\  & =(x+2)(x-4)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The factor $(x-4)$ has an exponent of $2$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=4$ has multiplicity $2.$
