questions.knowledge_point: Differentiating a Composition of Trigonometric Functions Using the Chain Rule
questions.problem: Find the derivative of $y=\operatorname{sin}(\operatorname{sec}x).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y=\operatorname{sin}u,\,u=\operatorname{sec}x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\operatorname{cos}u,\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sec}x\operatorname{tan}x.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}u\cdot (\operatorname{sec}x\operatorname{tan}x) \\  & =\operatorname{sec}x\operatorname{tan}x\operatorname{cos}(\operatorname{sec}x).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Velocity of a Particle at the Moment When Its Acceleration is Zero
questions.problem:
A particle $P$ is traveling along the $x$-axis with displacement $s(t)$ from a fixed origin $O$ given by

$$
s(t)=t{e}^{-t},\,t\ge 0.
$$

Find the time at which the acceleration is zero, and find the value of the velocity at this moment.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate $v(t)$ by differentiating $s(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t{e}^{-t}) \\  & =(1-t){e}^{-t}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we differentiate $v(t)$ to find $a(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}((1-t){e}^{-t}) \\  & =(t-2){e}^{-t}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we put $a=0$ to find the time when the acceleration is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =(t-2){e}^{-t} \\ t-2 & =0 \\ t & =2\end{aligned}
$$

So the acceleration is zero when $t=2.$ To find the velocity at this moment, we substitute this back into $v(t)$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(2) & =(1-(2)){e}^{-(2)} \\  & =-{e}^{-2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{{e}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving for a Constant Such that the Limit of a Piecewise Function Exists
questions.problem:
For the piecewise function 

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+2x+b\, & \text{ for }\,x\le 1 \\ {x}^{2}+cx+2\, & \text{ for }\,x>1\end{aligned}
$$

it is known that ${lim}_{x\to 1}f(x)=2.$ What is the value of the constants $b$ and $c?$
questions.worked_solution:
In order for ${lim}_{x\to 1}f(x)$ to be equal to $2,$ the left and right-sided limits must both exist and be equal to $2.$

- Approaching from the left, we have $x<1,$ so we use the expression $f(x)={x}^{2}+2x+b.$ We get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}({x}^{2}+2x+b) \\  & ={1}^{2}+2(1)+b \\  & =1+2+b \\  & =b+3\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the left-sided limit must be equal to $2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}f(x) & =2 \\ b+3 & =2 \\ b & =2-3 \\ b & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Approaching from the right, we have $x>1,$ so we use the expression $f(x)={x}^{2}+cx+2.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}({x}^{2}+cx+2) \\  & ={1}^{2}+c(1)+2 \\  & =1+c+2 \\  & =c+3\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the right-sided limit must be equal to $2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}f(x) & =2 \\ c+3 & =2 \\ c & =2-3 \\ c & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution to an Equation Containing a Transformed Reciprocal Function
questions.problem:
Consider the following trigonometric equation:

$$
\operatorname{sec}(\frac{x}{2}+\frac{\pi }{6})=-\sqrt{2}
$$

The general solution of this equation is

$$
x=\frac{7\pi }{6}+4\pi n,\,x=a+4\pi n,
$$

where $n$ is any integer. Which of the following could be the value of $a?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, note that the given equation is equivalent to

$$
\operatorname{cos}(\frac{x}{2}+\frac{\pi }{6})=-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.
$$

Therefore, the general solution to our equation is

$$
\frac{x}{2}+\frac{\pi }{6}=\frac{3\pi }{4}+2\pi n,\,\frac{x}{2}+\frac{\pi }{6}=\frac{5\pi }{4}+2\pi n.
$$

Solving the two equations above for $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{2}=-\frac{\pi }{6}+\frac{3\pi }{4}+2\pi n, & \,\frac{x}{2}=-\frac{\pi }{6}+\frac{5\pi }{4}+2\pi n \\ \frac{x}{2}=\frac{7\pi }{12}+2\pi n, & \,\frac{x}{2}=\frac{13\pi }{12}+2\pi n \\ x=\frac{7\pi }{6}+4\pi n, & \,x=\frac{13\pi }{6}+4\pi n.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have that $a=\frac{13\pi }{6}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Distance Between a Particle and the Origin
questions.problem: A particle starts moving from the point with position vector $4i\,\text{cm},$ with an acceleration of $(-2i+3j)\,{\text{cm/s}}^{2}$ and an initial velocity of $(2i+j)\,\text{cm/s}.$ Find the distance from the particle to the origin after $2$ seconds.
questions.worked_solution:
If a particle moves with constant acceleration $a,$ the position vector of the particle at time $t$ can be found using

$$
r={r}_{0}+ut+\frac{1}{2}a{t}^{2},
$$

 

where ${r}_{0}$ is the initial position of the particle and $u$ is its initial velocity.

In our case, we have

$$
{r}_{0}=4i,\,u=2i+j,\,a=-2i+3j.
$$

Therefore, the position vector of the particle after $t=2\,\text{s}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =(4i)+(2i+j)(2)+\frac{1}{2}(-2i+3j)(2)^{2} \\  & =(4i)+(4i+2j)+2(-2i+3j) \\  & =(8i+2j)+(-4i+6j) \\  & =(4i+8j)\,\text{cm}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the distance from the particle to the origin at this time is

$$
\begin{aligned}|r| & =|4i+8j| \\  & =\sqrt{{4}^{2}+{8}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16+64} \\  & =\sqrt{80} \\  & =4\sqrt{5}\,\text{cm}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Integrating a Linear Rational Function and Simplifying the Arbitrary Constant
questions.problem: Calculate $\int \frac{5}{3x+4}\,\text{d}x.$ Assume that $K$ is an arbitrary positive constant.
questions.worked_solution:
First, let $u=3x+4.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u.
$$

We can now rewrite the integral in terms of $u,$ solve it, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{5}{3x+4}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{5}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{5}{3}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{5}{3}\operatorname{ln}|u|+C \\  & =\frac{5}{3}\operatorname{ln}|3x+4|+C\end{aligned}
$$

We can further simplify the above by writing $C=\frac{5}{3}\operatorname{ln}K$ for another arbitrary positive constant $K,$ and then we can combine the two terms using the laws of logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{3}\operatorname{ln}|3x+4|+C & =\frac{5}{3}\operatorname{ln}|3x+4|+\frac{5}{3}\operatorname{ln}K \\  & =\frac{5}{3}(\operatorname{ln}|3x+4|+\operatorname{ln}K) \\  & =\frac{5}{3}\operatorname{ln}(K|3x+4|)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we finally conclude that

$$
\int \frac{5}{3x+4}\,\text{d}x=\frac{5}{3}\operatorname{ln}(K|3x+4|).
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Applying the Root Test in Divergent and Inconclusive Cases
questions.problem: Calculate $L={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}$ for the sequence ${a}_{n}=\frac{3{n}^{n}}{(1+n)^{n}}.$ According to the root test, does ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ converge or diverge?
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose we have the series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ such that ${a}_{n}\ge 0$ for all $n\ge 1,$ and that $L$ is defined as  

$$
L={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n}.
$$

 

Then, the root test states the following:

- If $L<1$, the series converges.

- If $L>1$ or $L=\infty $, the series diverges.

- If $L=1$, the root test is inconclusive.

We have the sequence ${a}_{n},$ defined as

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{3{n}^{n}}{(1+n)^{n}}.
$$

To apply the root test, we find the limit of $\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}$ as $n\to \infty :$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(\frac{3{n}^{n}}{(1+n)^{n}})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{\sqrt[n]{3}\,n}{1+n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{\sqrt[n]{3}\,n}{n(\frac{1}{n}+1)} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{\sqrt[n]{3}}{(\frac{1}{n}+1)} \\  & =\frac{1}{0+1} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used the fact that

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{3}=1.
$$

Since $L=1,$ the root test gives no conclusion.

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Slope of the Tangent Line of a Logarithmic Function at a Point
questions.problem: Given that $y=2{log}_{2}x+{2}^{x}$, find the slope of the tangent at $x=2.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the slope of the tangent at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2}{x\operatorname{ln}2}+{2}^{x}\operatorname{ln}2\,.
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent at $x=2$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=2} & ={(\frac{2}{x\operatorname{ln}2}+{2}^{x}\operatorname{ln}2)|}_{x=2} \\  & =\frac{2}{2\cdot \operatorname{ln}2}+{2}^{2}\operatorname{ln}2 \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}2}+4\operatorname{ln}2\,.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Expressing a Quotient of Complex Numbers in Polar Form
questions.problem: Express $z=\frac{6}{-1+\text{i}}$ in the form $r(\operatorname{cos}\theta +\text{i}\operatorname{sin}\theta ).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we express the given complex number in the form $z=x+y\text{i}.$ To do this, we remove $\text{i}$ from the denominator by multiplying the numerator and denominator of $z$ by the complex conjugate of the denominator, which is $-1-\text{i}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\frac{6}{-1+\text{i}} \\  & =\frac{6(-1-\text{i})}{(-1+\text{i})(-1-\text{i})} \\  & =\frac{6(-1-\text{i})}{(-1)^{2}-{\text{i}}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{6(-1-\text{i})}{1+1} \\  & =3(-1-\text{i}) \\  & =-3-3\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

 

In polar form, $r$ represents the magnitude $|z|.$ For a complex number $z=x+y\text{i},$ the magnitude of $z$ is given by

$$
|z|=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.
$$

So, for $z=-3-3\text{i},$ the magnitude is 

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-3)^{2}+(-3)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{18} \\  & =3\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

In polar form, $\theta $  represents the argument $\operatorname{arg}(z).$ Since $x=-3$ and $y=-3$ are both negative, $z$ lies in the third quadrant. So, we can find $\theta $ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}(z) & =\pi +\operatorname{arctan}|\frac{y}{x}| \\  & =\pi +\operatorname{arctan}|\frac{-3}{-3}| \\  & =\pi +\operatorname{arctan}1 \\  & =\pi +\frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =\frac{5\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the complex number $z$ in polar form:

$$
z=3\sqrt{2}(\operatorname{cos}(\frac{5\pi }{4})+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}(\frac{5\pi }{4}))
$$

$$

questions.knowledge_point: Analyzing Statements Involving Sums of Convergent Series
questions.problem:
Given that ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ is convergent and ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}$ is convergent, which of the following statements are true?

I. - ${\sum }_{n=100}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ is convergent
II. - ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}$ is divergent
III. - $1\,000{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}$ is convergent
questions.worked_solution:
Let's recall the properties of convergent series:

- If ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ is convergent, then ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }K\cdot {a}_{n}=K\cdot {\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ is also convergent.

- If ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ is convergent and ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}$ is convergent, then ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}$ is convergent.

- If ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ is convergent, then ${\sum }_{n=k}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ is also convergent.

With that in mind, let's analyze each statement:

- Statement I is true. Removing a finite number of terms from a convergent series gives a convergent series.

- Statement II is false. The sum of two convergent series is convergent.

- Statement III is true. Any constant multiple of a convergent series gives a convergent series.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

questions.problem: Simplify $\frac{{sin}^{2}x}{1-\operatorname{cos}x}-1$
questions.worked_solution:

$$
\frac{{sin}^{2}x}{1-\operatorname{cos}x}-1=\frac{1-{cos}^{2}x}{1-\operatorname{cos}x}-1
$$

Next, we factor the numerator of the first term as a difference of squares, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1-{cos}^{2}x}{1-\operatorname{cos}x}-1 & =\frac{(1-\operatorname{cos}x)(1+\operatorname{cos}x)}{1-\operatorname{cos}x}-1 \\  & =\frac{\cancel{(1-\operatorname{cos}x)}(1+\operatorname{cos}x)}{\cancel{1-\operatorname{cos}x}}-1 \\  & =\frac{1+\operatorname{cos}x}{1}-1 \\  & =1+\operatorname{cos}x-1 \\  & =\operatorname{cos}x\end{aligned}
$$

The sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of a geometric series is given by the formula

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r},\,|r|<1,
$$

where ${a}_{1}$ is the first term and $r$ is the common ratio.

From the question statement we have ${a}_{1}=56$ and ${a}_{3}=\frac{7}{8}.$ We can find the common ratio using the following formula:

$$
{r}^{n-m}=\frac{{a}_{n}}{{a}_{m}}
$$

Substituting in the known information into the above gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{3-1} & =\frac{(\frac{7}{8})}{56} \\ {r}^{2} & =(\frac{7}{8})(\frac{1}{56}) \\ {r}^{2} & =\frac{1}{64} \\ r & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{64}} \\ r & =\frac{1}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we have taken the positive square root since we're told that the sequence is positive.

So, using the formula, we find that the sum to infinity is

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{\infty } & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{56}{(1-\frac{1}{8})} \\  & =\frac{56}{(\frac{7}{8})} \\  & =56(\frac{8}{7}) \\  & =64.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Sum of a Geometric Series Given Two Consecutive Terms of the Series
questions.problem: The fifth term of a geometric series is $4$ and the sixth term is $2.$ What is the sum of the first $7$ terms?
questions.worked_solution:
The sum of the first $N$ terms of a geometric series is given by the formula

$$
{S}_{N}={a}_{1}\frac{(1-{r}^{N})}{1-r},
$$

where ${a}_{1}$ is the first term of the series, and $r$ is the common ratio.

To find $r,$ we find the ratio between the consecutive terms ${a}_{5}$ and ${a}_{6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\frac{{a}_{6}}{{a}_{5}} \\  & =\frac{2}{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now we must determine the value of ${a}_{1}.$ To do this, we use the formula for the $n$th term, which states that

$$
{a}_{n}={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1}.
$$

For $n=5,$ we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{5} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {(\frac{1}{2})}^{5-1} \\ 4 & ={a}_{1}\cdot {(\frac{1}{2})}^{4} \\ 4 & ={a}_{1}\cdot \frac{1}{16} \\ {a}_{1} & =\frac{4}{(\frac{1}{16})} \\ {a}_{1} & =64\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, if we substitute ${a}_{1}=64,N=7$ and $r=\frac{1}{2}$ into the formula for ${S}_{N},$ we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{7} & =64\cdot \frac{1-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{7}}{1-\frac{1}{2}} \\  & =64\cdot \frac{1-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{7}}{\frac{1}{2}} \\  & =\frac{64}{(\frac{1}{2})}\cdot (1-\frac{1}{128}) \\  & =128(1-\frac{1}{128}) \\  & =128-1 \\  & =127\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving an Elementary Quadratic Inequality by Manipulating the Inequality First
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's simplify the inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2} & \ge 27-2{x}^{2} \\ {x}^{2}+2{x}^{2} & \ge 27 \\ 3{x}^{2} & \ge 27 \\ {x}^{2} & \ge 9\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can use either of two methods to solve the inequality.

*Method 1 - Solving an Absolute Value Equation*

Taking the square root of both sides of the inequality, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2} & \ge 9 \\ \sqrt{{x}^{2}} & \ge \sqrt{9} \\ |x| & \ge 3.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the definition of absolute value, we must have 

$$
x\le -3\,\text{or}\,x\ge 3.
$$

So, the solution is $\,x\in (-\infty ,-3]\cup [3,\infty ).$

*Method 2 - Picturing a Quadratic Curve*

Starting from ${x}^{2}\ge 9$ and moving all terms to the left-hand side, we reach

$$
{x}^{2}-9\ge 0.
$$

Now, we consider the corresponding parabola given by $y={x}^{2}-9$ and find its roots:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-9 & =0 \\ {x}^{2} & =9 \\ x & =\pm \sqrt{9} \\  & =\pm 3\end{aligned}
$$

So the roots are $x=\pm 3.$ 

Since the leading coefficient of ${x}^{2}-9$ is positive, the parabola opens upward. Therefore, the solution to the given inequality ($y\ge 0$) lies outside the roots (and include them).

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/history-question-import-2026-10-04/import-ready/assets/f277a8b22194fae2d932f6f39ac28e869955486820c195f5e027a9bc49cd493c.png)

Therefore, the solution is $x\in (-\infty ,-3]\cup [3,\infty ).$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving Rational Equations Containing Quadratic Denominators
questions.problem: Which value of $y$ satisfies the equation $\frac{y+1}{{y}^{2}}=\frac{3}{2y}+\frac{2y-1}{{y}^{2}}?$
questions.worked_solution:
We note that $y=0$ cannot be a solution since division by $0$ is undefined. 

The equation has the denominators ${y}^{2}$ and $2y.$ So first, we find the least common multiple (or $\text{LCM}$) of the denominators. We find that

$$
\text{LCM}({y}^{2},2y)=2{y}^{2}.
$$

So, we multiply both sides of the equation by $2{y}^{2},$ and simplify: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y+1}{{y}^{2}} & =\frac{3}{2y}+\frac{2y-1}{{y}^{2}} \\ 2{y}^{2}\cdot (\frac{y+1}{{y}^{2}}) & =2{y}^{2}\cdot (\frac{3}{2y}+\frac{2y-1}{{y}^{2}}) \\ 2{y}^{2}\cdot (\frac{y+1}{{y}^{2}}) & =2{y}^{2}\cdot (\frac{3}{2y})+2{y}^{2}\cdot (\frac{2y-1}{{y}^{2}}) \\ 2\cdot {y}^{2}\cdot (\frac{y+1}{{y}^{2}}) & =y\cdot 2y\cdot (\frac{3}{2y})+2\cdot {y}^{2}\cdot (\frac{2y-1}{{y}^{2}}) \\ 2\cdot \cancel{{y}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{y+1}{\cancel{{y}^{2}}}) & =y\cdot \cancel{2y}\cdot (\frac{3}{\cancel{2y}})+2\cdot \cancel{{y}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{2y-1}{\cancel{{y}^{2}}}) \\ 2(y+1) & =3y+2(2y-1)\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $y,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}2(y+1) & =3y+2(2y-1) \\ 2y+2 & =7y-2 \\ 7y-2y & =2+2 \\ 5y & =4 \\ y & =\frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $y=0$ as a solution. But since $y=\frac{4}{5}\ne 0,$ we conclude that the solution is $y=\frac{4}{5}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving an Exponential Equation by Rearranging the Equation and Then Factoring
questions.problem: What is the product of solutions of the equation $4{x}^{2}{e}^{5x}=3{e}^{5x}-4x{e}^{5x}?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we factor the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}{e}^{5x} & =3{e}^{5x}-4x{e}^{5x} \\ 4{x}^{2}{e}^{5x}+4x{e}^{5x}-3{e}^{5x} & =0 \\ (4{x}^{2}+4x-3){e}^{5x} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

We can now apply the zero product property, which states that $ab=0$ if and only if $a=0$ or $b=0.$ This gives us two equations,

$$
4{x}^{2}+4x-3=0\,\text{and}\,{e}^{5x}=0.
$$

We now solve each of these equations separately.

- The equation $4{x}^{2}+4x-3=0$ can be factored as

$$
(2x+3)(2x-1)=0,
$$

which leads to the solutions $x=-\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2}.$

- The equation ${e}^{5x}=0$ has no solutions because ${e}^{5x}$ is positive for every real number $x.$

Therefore, the original equation has the solutions $x=-\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2},$ and their product is $(-\frac{3}{2})\cdot \frac{1}{2}=-\frac{3}{4}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Left Riemann Sum With Irregular Step Size
questions.problem:
The following table shows some values of a continuous function $f(x)$ over the interval $[2,12].$

| $x$ | $2$ | $4$ | $8$ | $10$ | $12$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $5$ | $3$ | $2$ | $1$ | $1$ |

Use the left Riemann sum, with the four subintervals indicated by the data, to approximate the area under the curve $y=f(x)$ over the interval $[2,12].$
questions.worked_solution:
In this case, we have $n=4$ rectangles. Using the left Riemann sum, the area is approximated as

$$
A\approx f(2)Δ{x}_{1}+f(4)Δ{x}_{2}+f(8)Δ{x}_{3}+f(10)Δ{x}_{4},
$$

where each $Δ{x}_{i}$ is calculated by considering the step between a particular $x$-value and the next one, i.e.,

$$
Δ{x}_{i}={x}_{i+1}-{x}_{i}.
$$

We set up a value table that includes the $Δx$'s.

| $x$ | $2$ | $4$ | $8$ | $10$ | $12$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $Δx$ | $2$ | $4$ | $2$ | $2$ | $-$ |
| $f(x)$ | $5$ | $3$ | $2$ | $1$ | $1$ |

Finally, we plug in the numbers to approximate the area under the curve and get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & \approx 5\cdot 2+3\cdot 4+2\cdot 2+1\cdot 2 \\  & =10+12+4+2 \\  & =28.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining Convergence Behavior of Geometric Sequences Written Recursively
questions.problem:
Consider the following sequence: 

$$
{a}_{n+1}=-\frac{5}{4}{a}_{n},\,{a}_{1}=\frac{1}{2},\,n\ge 1.
$$

Determine whether the sequence is convergent or divergent. If it converges, find the limit.
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a geometric sequence with the first term ${a}_{1}$ and common ratio $r.$ Then, we have the following convergence properties:

- if $|r|<1,$ the sequence is convergent and converges to $0$

- if $|r|>1,$ the sequence is divergent

Moreover, we have the following edge cases:

- if $r=1,$ the sequence is convergent and converges to ${a}_{1}$

- if $r=-1,$ the sequence is divergent

The given sequence is a geometric sequence with the common ratio 

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}=-\frac{5}{4}.
$$

Since $|r|>1$, the sequence diverges.

questions.problem: Given that ${e}^{6w+3}+7=11,$ then $w=$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange our equation into a form that is more convenient for logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{6w+3}+7=11 \\ {e}^{6w+3} & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we find the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation and solve for $w:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{6w+3} & =4 \\ \operatorname{ln}({e}^{6w+3}) & =\operatorname{ln}(4) \\ 6w+3 & =\operatorname{ln}(4) \\ 6w & =\operatorname{ln}(4)-3 \\ w & =\frac{1}{6}(\operatorname{ln}(4)-3)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $w=\frac{1}{6}(\operatorname{ln}(4)-3).$

questions.knowledge_point: Multiplying Two Complex Numbers
questions.problem: $(6-9\,\text{i})(3+7\,\text{i})=$ ${{real-part}}+{{imaginary-coefficient}}\,\mathrm{i}$
questions.worked_solution:
Multiplying two complex numbers is similar to multiplying two binomials. We also use the fact that ${\text{i}}^{2}=-1.$

For the given problem, we have

$$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving Logarithmic Equations by Combining Logarithmic Terms
questions.problem: If ${log}_{8}x+2{log}_{8}x=2$, then what is the value of  $x?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange our equation to isolate the logarithmic term:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{8}x+2{log}_{8}x & =2 \\ (1+2){log}_{8}x & =2 \\ 3{log}_{8}x & =2 \\ {log}_{8}x & =\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

To remove the logarithm, we exponentiate both sides of the equation. The base of the logarithm is $8,$ so we use this base for the exponentiation as well:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{8}x & =\frac{2}{3} \\ {8}^{{log}_{8}x} & ={8}^{2/3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we get ${8}^{{log}_{8}x}=x.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={8}^{2/3} \\ x & =\sqrt[3]{64} \\ x & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find $|r(\frac{\pi }{3})|$ given that $r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}t,\,4\operatorname{sin}t,\,6⟩.$
questions.worked_solution:
Evaluating the function at $t=\frac{\pi }{3},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(\frac{\pi }{3}) & =⟨2\operatorname{cos}(\frac{\pi }{3}),\,4\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{3}),\,6⟩ \\  & =⟨2\cdot \frac{1}{2},\,4\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},\,6⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,2\sqrt{3},\,6⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the magnitude of this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|r(\frac{\pi }{3})| & =\sqrt{{(1)}^{2}+{(2\sqrt{3})}^{2}+(6)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+12+36} \\  & =\sqrt{49} \\  & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving Systems With Two Quadratic Equations
questions.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}x=3{y}^{2}-4y \\ 8x-7{y}^{2}=5x\end{aligned}
$$

If $(x,y)$ is a solution of the system above such that $x\ne 0$, what is the value of $x+y?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we simplify the second equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}8x-7{y}^{2} & =5x \\ 3x-7{y}^{2} & =0 \\ 3x & =7{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, from the first equation, we have

$$
x=3{y}^{2}-4y.
$$

We substitute this into the second equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x & =7{y}^{2} \\ 3(3{y}^{2}-4y) & =7{y}^{2} \\ 9{y}^{2}-12y & =7{y}^{2} \\ 2{y}^{2}-12y & =0 \\ {y}^{2}-6y & =0 \\ y(y-6) & =0 \\ y & =0,\,6\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute $y$ in the first equation.

- For ${y}_{1}=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =3{y}_{1}^{2}-4{y}_{1} \\  & =3(0)^{2}-4(0) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- For ${y}_{2}=6,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =3{y}_{2}^{2}-4{y}_{2} \\  & =3(6)^{2}-4(6) \\  & =108-24 \\  & =84.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are 

$$
({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(0,0)\,\text{and}\,({x}_{2},{y}_{2})=(84,6).
$$

Finally, since we require the solution such that $x\ne 0,$ we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y & ={x}_{2}+{y}_{2} \\  & =84+6 \\  & =90.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Properties of Platonic Solids
questions.problem:
Which of the following statements must be true regarding any tetrahedron? 

I. - It has $4$ congruent faces, each in the form of a right triangle
II. - Exactly $3$ faces meet at each vertex
III. - It has $4$ edges
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/history-question-import-2026-10-04/import-ready/assets/adcc202ad86b782fd153566d6454269dcd50e8f1d9aca37bc42d2266c142ced8.png)

Let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false, while statement II is true. A tetrahedron is a regular polyhedron that 

- consists of $4$ congruent faces, each in the form of an equilateral triangle (not a right triangle), and

- exactly $3$ faces meet at each vertex.

- Statement III is false. Since there are $F=4$ faces, each in the form of an equilateral triangle, we have

$$
S=4\cdot 3=12
$$

sides combined. Now, each edge of the polyhedron is created when two face sides coincide. So, the number of edges of the tetrahedron must be equal to

$$
\frac{S}{2}=\frac{12}{2}=6.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Point That Lies on a Transformed Curve Given Another Transformed Curve
questions.problem: The point  $(0,1)$ lies on the curve $y=f(x+2).$ Which of the following points **must** lie on $y=-f(x)+2?$
questions.worked_solution:
**Method 1**

We first find a point corresponding to $(0,1)$ on $y=f(x).$ Then, we find a corresponding point on $y=-f(x)+2:$

- To plot the graph of $y=f(x),$ we apply the following steps:

- First, take the graph $y=f(x+2).$

- Then, we shift the graph horizontally $2$ unit to the right  and get the graph of $y=f(x).$ After this transformation, the point $(0,1)$ will be mapped to the point

$$
(0+2,1)=(2,1).
$$

- Next, to plot the graph of $y=-f(x)+2,$ we apply the following steps:

- First, take the graph $y=f(x).$

- Then, we reflect the result across the $x$-axis and get the graph of $y=-f(x).$ After this transformation, the point $(2,1)$ will be mapped  to the point

$$
(2,-(1))=(2,-1).
$$

- Next, we shift the result vertically by $2$ units up and obtain the graph of $y=-f(x)+2.$ After this transformation, the point $(2,-1)$ will be mapped to the point 

$$
(2,-1+2)=(2,1).
$$

**Method 2**

Since the point $(0,1)$ lies on the graph of $y=f(x+2)$, we have that 

$$
f(0+2)=1\,⟹\,f(2)=1.
$$

Now consider the graph of $y=-f(x)+2.$ Substituting $x=2$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-f(2)+2 \\  & =-(1)+2 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the point $(2,1)$ must lie on $y=-f(x)+2.$

questions.problem: The point  $(2,1)$ lies on the curve $y=f(x-2).$ Which of the following points **must** lie on $y=3-f(x)?$
questions.worked_solution:
**Method 1**

We first find a point corresponding to $(2,1)$ on $y=f(x).$ Then, we find a corresponding point on $y=3-f(x):$

- To plot the graph of $y=f(x),$ we apply the following steps:

- First, take the graph $y=f(x-2).$

- Then, we shift the graph horizontally $2$ units to the left and get the graph of $y=f(x).$ After this transformation, the point $(2,1)$ will be mapped to the point

$$
(2-2,1)=(0,1).
$$

- Next, to plot the graph of $y=3-f(x),$ we apply the following steps:

- First, take the graph $y=f(x).$

- Then, we reflect the result across the $x$-axis and get the graph of $y=-f(x).$ After this transformation, the point $(0,1)$ will be mapped  to the point

$$
(0,-(1))=(0,-1).
$$

- Next, we shift the result vertically by $3$ units up and obtain the graph of $y=3-f(x).$ After this transformation, the point $(0,-1)$ will be mapped to the point 

$$
(0,-1+3)=(0,2).
$$

**Method 2**

Since the point $(2,1)$ lies on the graph of $y=f(x-2)$, we have that 

$$
f(2-2)=1\,⟹\,f(0)=1.
$$

Now consider the graph of $y=3-f(x).$ Substituting $x=0$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =3-f(0) \\  & =3-1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the point $(0,2)$ must lie on $y=3-f(x).$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Extrema on Transformed Curves
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/history-question-import-2026-10-04/import-ready/assets/282e65324ea1e7893da25ead1cc822c7c166df880c3aecc60face9adbbb7279a.png)

The diagram above shows the local minimum and maximum of the function $y=f(x).$ What is the local maximum of $y=f(x+3)-2?$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that the graph of $y=f(x+3)-2$ can be obtained from the graph of $y=f(x)$ by 

- translating it by $3$ units to the left, and then

- translating it by $2$ unit down.

Since these transformations do not flip the graph across the $x$-axis, the combined transformation maps the local maximum of $y=f(x)$ to the local maximum of $y=f(x+3)-2.$ So, we need to find the image of $(-2,6),$ the local maximum of $y=f(x),$ under the transformation. 

To plot $y=f(x+3)-2,$ we apply the following steps: 

- First, we take the graph $y=f(x)$ that passes through $(-2,6).$

- Then, we shift the graph horizontally by $3$ units to the left and get the graph of $y=f(x+3).$ After this transformation, the point $(-2,6)$ will be mapped to the point

$$
(-2-3,6)=(-5,6).
$$

- Finally, we shift the result vertically by $2$ units downward and get the graph of $y=f(x+3)-2.$ After this transformation, the point $(-5,6)$ will be mapped to the point

$$
(-5,6-2)=(-5,4).
$$

Therefore, the local maximum of $y=f(x+3)-2$ is $(-5,4).$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Tangent or Cotangent of a Special Angle
questions.problem: $\operatorname{tan}(\frac{11\pi }{6})=$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's remind ourselves of the special trigonometric ratios, as given by the unit circle.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/history-question-import-2026-10-04/import-ready/assets/dbf36192ac332dc49ed75278838e989a37ac7d888311be1b8b059a7b59667aa6.png)

From the unit circle, we see that the angle $\frac{11\pi }{6}$ corresponds to the point $(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},-\frac{1}{2}).$

- Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the $x$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{cos}(\frac{11\pi }{6})=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.$

- Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the $y$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{sin}(\frac{11\pi }{6})=-\frac{1}{2}.$

Therefore, using the fact that $\operatorname{tan}\theta =\frac{\operatorname{sin}\theta }{\operatorname{cos}\theta },$ we have

$$
\operatorname{tan}(\frac{11\pi }{6})=\frac{\operatorname{sin}(\frac{11\pi }{6})}{\operatorname{cos}(\frac{11\pi }{6})}=\frac{(-\frac{1}{2})}{(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})}=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}.
$$

questions.problem: Calculate the integral $\int \frac{{2}^{z}}{\sqrt{{2}^{z}-9}}\,\text{d}z.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{2}^{z}}{\sqrt{{2}^{z}-9}}\,\text{d}z & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{2}^{z}-9}}\cdot {2}^{z}\,\text{d}z \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}2}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}2}\int {u}^{-1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}2}\cdot \frac{{u}^{1/2}}{(\frac{1}{2})} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{{2}^{z}-9}}{\operatorname{ln}2}+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Cubic Polynomial Given One Real Root, Two Complex Roots, and a Leading Coefficient
questions.problem: The cubic polynomial $f(x)$ has roots ${x}_{1}=-2,{x}_{2,3}=1\pm 2\text{i},$ and the coefficient of the cubic term is $3.$ Find $f(x).$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $f(x)$ has roots ${x}_{1}=-2$ and ${x}_{2,3}=1\pm 2\text{i},$ and the coefficient of the cubic term is $a=3,$ we can write the polynomial as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =a(x-{x}_{1})(x-{x}_{2})(x-{x}_{3}) \\  & =3(x-(-2))(x-(1+2\text{i}))(x-(1-2\text{i})) \\  & =3(x+2)(x-(1+2\text{i}))(x-(1-2\text{i}))\end{aligned}
$$

Expanding the parentheses, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}3(x+2)(x-(1+2\text{i}))(x-(1-2\text{i})) & = \\ 3(x+2)({x}^{2}-x(1+2\text{i})-x(1-2\text{i})+(1+2\text{i})(1-2\text{i})) & = \\ 3(x+2)({x}^{2}-2x+5) & = \\ 3({x}^{3}+2{x}^{2}-2{x}^{2}-4x+5x+10) & = \\ 3({x}^{3}+x+10) & = \\ 3{x}^{3}+3x+30 & .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)=3{x}^{3}+3x+30.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Roots of a Rational Function With Common Factors
questions.problem: Find the roots of $f(w)=\frac{{w}^{2}-3w-10}{2{w}^{2}-10w}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The roots of $f(w)$ are the solutions to the equation $f(w)=0.$ In our case, we have

$$
\frac{{w}^{2}-3w-10}{2{w}^{2}-10w}=0.
$$

First, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(w) & =\frac{{w}^{2}-3w-10}{2{w}^{2}-10w} \\  & =\frac{(w+2)(w-5)}{2w(w-5)} \\  & =\frac{(w+2)\cancel{(w-5)}}{2w\cancel{(w-5)}} \\  & =\frac{(w+2)}{2w}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set the numerator equal to zero and solve for $w:$

$$
\begin{aligned}w+2 & =0\,⟹\,w=-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to $f(w)=0$ is $w=-2.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2{x}^{2}-4x}{{x}^{2}-x-2} & =\frac{2x(x-2)}{(x-2)(x+1)} \\  & =\frac{2x\cancel{(x-2)}}{\cancel{(x-2)}(x+1)} \\  & =\frac{2x}{x+1}\end{aligned}
$$

We now set the denominator equal to zero:

$$
x+1=0\,⟹\,x=-1
$$

So the *only* vertical asymptote is at $x=-1.$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Vertical Asymptotes With Common Factors in the Numerator and Denominator
questions.problem: Find the vertical asymptotes of $f(x)=\frac{{x}^{2}-x-2}{{x}^{3}+7{x}^{2}-x-7}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the vertical asymptotes of a rational function, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors. Then, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x.$

Factoring the numerator and denominator and canceling any common factors, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{{x}^{2}-x-2}{{x}^{3}+7{x}^{2}-x-7} \\  & =\frac{(x-2)(x+1)}{{x}^{2}(x+7)-(x+7)} \\  & =\frac{(x-2)(x+1)}{({x}^{2}-1)(x+7)} \\  & =\frac{(x-2)(x+1)}{(x-1)(x+1)(x+7)} \\  & =\frac{(x-2)\cancel{(x+1)}}{(x-1)\cancel{(x+1)}(x+7)} \\  & =\frac{x-2}{(x-1)(x+7)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x:$

$$
(x-1)(x+7)=0
$$

This gives the two solutions $x=-7$ and $x=1.$ Therefore, the equations of the vertical asymptotes are $x=-7$ and $x=1.$

questions.problem: Write the equation of the hyperbola $4{y}^{2}-5{x}^{2}=40$ in standard form.
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of a vertical hyperbola centered at the origin is

$$
\frac{{y}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

Therefore, to write the equation of the hyperbola in standard form, we need to divide both sides of the equation by $40$ and then simplify, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{y}^{2}-5{x}^{2} & =40 \\ \frac{4{y}^{2}}{40}-\frac{5{x}^{2}}{40} & =\frac{40}{40} \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{10}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{8} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Choosing a Parameter to Force a Desired Number of Solutions to a Quadratic Equation
questions.problem: Find the values of $k$ for which the quadratic equation $5{x}^{2}+15x+k=0$ has one distinct real solution.
questions.worked_solution:
The equation has one distinct real solution if its discriminant is zero. So, we need to find the values of $k$ so that the discriminant is zero.

First, we calculate the discriminant. We have $a=5,$ $b=15,$ and $c=k,$ so the discriminant is as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}D & ={b}^{2}-4ac \\  & =(15)^{2}-4(5)(k) \\  & =225-20k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the values of $k$ such that the discriminant is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}D & =0 \\ 225-20k & =0 \\ 20k & =225 \\ k & =\frac{225}{20} \\ k & =\frac{45}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the given equation will have one distinct real solution if $k=\frac{45}{4}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Root of a Transformed Exponential Function
questions.problem: Find the root of $f(x)=2(5)^{3x+2}-54.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the root of $f(x),$  we must solve $f(x)=0:$

$$
2(5)^{3x+2}-54=0
$$

First, we isolate the term with the variable exponent by adding $54$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}2(5)^{3x+2}-54 & =0 \\ 2(5)^{3x+2}-\cancel{54}+\cancel{54} & =0+54 \\ 2(5)^{3x+2} & =54\end{aligned}
$$

Dividing both sides by $2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2(5)^{3x+2} & =54 \\ {5}^{3x+2} & =27.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we rewrite $27$ as ${3}^{3}$ to get

$$
{5}^{3x+2}={3}^{3}.
$$

Then we take ${log}_{5}$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{5}^{3x+2} & ={3}^{3} \\ {log}_{5}({5}^{3x+2}) & ={log}_{5}({3}^{3}) \\ 3x+2 & =3{log}_{5}(3)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x+2 & =3{log}_{5}(3) \\ 3x & =3{log}_{5}(3)-2 \\ x & =\frac{3{log}_{5}(3)-2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Index of a Term Given the Recursive Formula
questions.problem:
What is the index of the term $-75$ for the arithmetic sequence below?

$$
{a}_{n+1}={a}_{n}-3,\,{a}_{1}=-3,\,n\ge 1
$$

Answer: {{answer}}
questions.worked_solution:
We will convert the recursive formula to an explicit formula and then solve for the value of $n$ such that ${a}_{n}=-75.$

The recursive rule for an arithmetic sequence takes the form

$$
{a}_{n+1}={a}_{n}+d.
$$

In the given formula, we have $d=-3.$ We are also told that ${a}_{1}=-3,$ so we can write the explicit formula as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}+(n-1)d \\  & =-3+(n-1)(-3) \\  & =-3-3n+3 \\  & =-3n\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for the value of $n$ such that ${a}_{n}=-75:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =-3n \\ -75 & =-3n \\ \frac{-75}{-3} & =n \\ 25 & =n\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $-75$ is the $25$th term of the sequence.

questions.problem: $\operatorname{sec}(\frac{2\pi }{3})=$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's remind ourselves of the special trigonometric ratios, as given by the unit circle.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/history-question-import-2026-10-04/import-ready/assets/dbf36192ac332dc49ed75278838e989a37ac7d888311be1b8b059a7b59667aa6.png)

From the unit circle, we see that the angle $\frac{2\pi }{3}$ corresponds to the point $(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}).$

Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the $x$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{cos}(\frac{2\pi }{3})=-\frac{1}{2}.$

Therefore, using the fact that $\operatorname{sec}\theta =\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}\theta },$ we have

$$
\operatorname{sec}(\frac{2\pi }{3})=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}(\frac{2\pi }{3})}=-2.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Vector From Position Vectors and then Computing its Magnitude
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/history-question-import-2026-10-04/import-ready/assets/f35a3ad730621023ec86e5727588fc86083ee500b3a72c55ab2808bd290019e9.png)

Let $P(1,2)$ and $Q(-2,1).$ Find $|\overset{\to }{PQ}|.$
questions.worked_solution:
We have 

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{OP}=p=i+2j, \\  & \overset{\to }{OQ}=q=-2i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ as the difference of position vectors, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =\overset{\to }{OQ}-\overset{\to }{OP} \\  & =q-p \\  & =(-2i+j)-(i+2j) \\  & =-3i-j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the formula for the magnitude of a vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|\overset{\to }{PQ}| & =\sqrt{(-3)^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9+1} \\  & =\sqrt{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Point That Lies on a Transformed Curve
questions.problem: The point $(-1,1)$ lies on the curve $y=f(x).$ Which of the following points **must** lie on $y=3f(x+2)?$
questions.worked_solution:
**Method 1**

To plot $y=3f(x+2),$ we apply the following steps: 

- First, we take the graph $y=f(x).$

- Then, shift the graph horizontally by $2$ unit to the left and get the graph of 
$y=f(x+2).$  After this transformation, the point $(-1,1)$ will be mapped to the point

$$
(-1-2,1)=(-3,1).
$$

- Finally, we stretch the result by a scale factor of $3$ parallel to the y-axis and get the graph of 
$y=3f(x+2).$ After this transformation, the point $(-3,1)$ will be mapped to the point

$$
(-3,3\cdot 1)=(-3,3).
$$

**Method 2**

Since the point $(-1,1)$ lies on the graph of $y=f(x)$, we have that $f(-1)=1.$

Now consider the graph of $y=3f(x+2).$ Substituting $x=-3$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =3f(-3+2) \\  & =3f(-1) \\  & =3\cdot 1 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the point $(-3,3)$ must lie on $y=3f(x+2).$

$$

Therefore, we have that ${\text{i}}^{2}=-1.$

questions.problem: The length of a rectangular solid is $8\,\text{yd}$ and its volume is $392\,{\text{yd}}^{3}.$ If the side face (width x height) of the solid is a square, find the width of the solid.
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the volume $V$ of the rectangular prism using the formula

$$
V=lwh,
$$

where $l$ is the length, $w$ is the width, and $h$ is the height of the solid.

Since the side face of the rectangular solid is a square, we have that 

$$
w=h.
$$

Substituting 

$$
V=392,\,l=8,\,h=w
$$

into the formula, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =lwh \\ V & =l{w}^{2} \\ 392 & =8\cdot {w}^{2} \\ {w}^{2} & =49 \\ w & =7\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the width is $7\,\text{yd}.$

The diagram above shows a milk carton. Three-eighths of the carton is filled with milk, forming a cube. Find the volume of the empty space in the carton.
questions.worked_solution:
The milk in the carton creates a cube. Since the height of the milk is $3\,\text{in},$ the side length of the cube is also $3\,\text{in}.$

Also, the height of $3\,\text{in}$ shown in the diagram represents three-eighths of the carton's height. Therefore, the height of the carton is

$$
\frac{8}{3}\cdot 3=8\,\text{in}.
$$

The empty space in the carton is a rectangular prism that is $3\,\text{in}$ long, $3\,\text{in}$ wide, and $8-3=5\,\text{in}$ high.

We can find the volume $V$ of the rectangular prism using the formula

$$
V=lwh,
$$

where $l$ is the length, $w$ is the width, and $h$ is the height of the solid.

Substituting 

$$
l=3\,\text{in},\,w=3\,\text{in},\,h=5\,\text{in}
$$

into the formula, we obtain

$$
V=3\cdot 3\cdot 5=45\,{\text{in}}^{3}.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that there is $45\,{\text{in}}^{3}$ of empty space in the carton.

What is the length of $\overset{―}{AB}?$
questions.worked_solution:
From the figure, we note that the points $A$ and $B$ have coordinates ${{(1,5)}_{⏟}}_{\text{(}{x}_{1}\text{,}\,{y}_{1})}$ and ${{(6,2)}_{⏟}}_{\text{(}{x}_{2}\text{,}\,{y}_{2})},$ respectively. 

To find the distance $AB,$ we can use the distance formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}AB & =\sqrt{({x}_{2}-{x}_{1})^{2}+({y}_{2}-{y}_{1})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(6-1)^{2}+(2-5)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{5}^{2}+(-3)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25+9} \\  & =\sqrt{34}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Distance Between Two Points
questions.problem: What is the distance between the points $(-1,1)$ and $(-3,-2)?$
questions.worked_solution:
In this case, we have ${{(-1,1)}_{⏟}}_{\text{(}{x}_{1}\text{,}\,{y}_{1})}$ and ${{(-3,-2)}_{⏟}}_{\text{(}{x}_{2}\text{,}\,{y}_{2})}.$ 
So, the distance $d$ can be calculated using the distance formula, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\sqrt{({x}_{2}-{x}_{1})^{2}+({y}_{2}-{y}_{1})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-3-(-1))^{2}+(-2-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+(-3)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4+9} \\  & =\sqrt{13}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Discriminant of a Quadratic Equation
questions.problem: Calculate the discriminant of the quadratic equation $2(x+2)^{2}-3=0.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}2(x+2)^{2}-3 & =2({x}^{2}+4x+{2}^{2})-3 \\  & =2{x}^{2}+8x+8-3 \\  & =2{x}^{2}+8x+5.\end{aligned}
$$

We have $a=2,$ $b=8,$ and $c=5.$ So, we calculate the discriminant as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}D & ={b}^{2}-4ac \\  & ={8}^{2}-4(2)(5) \\  & =64-40 \\  & =24\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the equation $-{x}^{2}-2x+7=0.$ How many distinct real solutions does it have?
questions.worked_solution:
To quickly determine the number of solutions, we can compute the discriminant. We have $a=-1,$ $b=-2,$ and $c=7,$ so the discriminant is as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}D & ={b}^{2}-4ac \\  & =(-2)^{2}-4(-1)(7) \\  & =4+28 \\  & =32\end{aligned}
$$

Since the discriminant is positive $(D>0),$ the equation has two distinct real solutions.

questions.knowledge_point: Choosing a Parameter to Force a Desired Number of Solutions to a Quadratic Equation
questions.problem: Find the values of $k$ for which the quadratic equation $-15{x}^{2}+kx-60=0$  has one distinct real solution.
questions.worked_solution:
The equation has one distinct real solution if its discriminant is zero. So, we need to find the values of $k$ so that the discriminant is zero.

First, we calculate the discriminant. We have $a=-15,$ $b=k,$ and $c=-60,$ so the discriminant is as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}D & ={b}^{2}-4ac \\  & =(k)^{2}-4(-15)(-60) \\  & ={k}^{2}-3\,600\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the values of $k$ such that the discriminant is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}D=0 \\ {k}^{2}-3600 & =0 \\ {k}^{2} & =3600 \\ k & =\pm \sqrt{3600} \\ k & =\pm 60\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the given equation will have one distinct real solution if $k=\pm 60.$

questions.knowledge_point: Choosing a Parameter to Force a Desired Number of Solutions to a Quadratic Equation
questions.problem: Find the values of $k$ for which the quadratic equation ${x}^{2}-4x+k=0$ has two distinct real solutions.
questions.worked_solution:
The equation has two distinct real solutions if its discriminant is positive. So, we need to find the values of $k$ so that the discriminant is positive.

First, we calculate the discriminant. We have $a=1,$ $b=-4$ and $c=k,$ so the discriminant is as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}D & ={b}^{2}-4ac \\  & =(-4)^{2}-4(1)(k) \\  & =16-4k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the values of $k$ such that the discriminant is positive:

$$
\begin{aligned}D & >0 \\ 16-4k & >0 \\ 16 & >4k \\ 4k & <16 \\ k & <4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the given equation will have two distinct real solutions if $k<4.$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Quadratic Equations With Rational Solutions
questions.problem:
Consider the quadratic equation $\frac{1}{4}{x}^{2}+3x+5=0.$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. - The discriminant of the equation is a perfect square.
II. - The equation has only rational solutions.
III. - The equation has only irrational solutions.
questions.worked_solution:
Let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. We have $a=\frac{1}{4},$ $b=3,$ and $c=5.$ So, we calculate the discriminant as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}D & ={b}^{2}-4ac \\  & =(3)^{2}-4(\frac{1}{4})(5) \\  & =9-5 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

And $4={2}^{2}$ is a perfect square.

- Statement II is true, while statement III is false. 

First, notice that our quadratic equation has rational coefficients. And, since the discriminant is a nonzero perfect square, the equation must have two rational solutions.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

questions.problem:
Consider the quadratic equation $2{x}^{2}+x-4=0.$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. - The discriminant of the equation is a perfect square.
II. - The equation has only rational solutions.
III. - The equation has only irrational solutions.
questions.worked_solution:
Let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. We have $a=2,$ $b=1,$ and $c=-4.$ So, we calculate the discriminant as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}D & ={b}^{2}-4ac \\  & =(1)^{2}-4(2)(-4) \\  & =1+32 \\  & =33\end{aligned}
$$

And $33$ is *not* a perfect square.

- Statement II is false, while statement III is true.

First, notice that our quadratic equation has rational coefficients. And, since the discriminant is not a perfect square, the equation must have two irrational solutions.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

$$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving Rational Equations with Binomials in Both Denominators
questions.problem: Solve the equation $-\frac{2}{x+3}=\frac{8}{x-1}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we note that

- $x=-3$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero

- $x=1$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
-\frac{x+3}{2}=\frac{x-1}{8}
$$

Next, we write both fractions using the least common denominator, $8.$ The equation becomes

$$
-\frac{4x+12}{8}=\frac{x-1}{8}.
$$

We can now solve this equation with the addition and the multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-8)\cdot \frac{4x+12}{-8} & =(-8)\cdot \frac{x-1}{8} \\ 4x+12 & =-x+1 \\ 4x+x & =1-12 \\ 5x & =-11 \\ (\frac{1}{5})\cdot (5x) & =(\frac{1}{5})\cdot (-11) \\ (\cancel{\frac{1}{5}})\cdot (\cancel{5}x) & =(\frac{1}{5})\cdot (-11) \\ x & =-\frac{11}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/history-question-import-2026-10-04/import-ready/assets/01509c920e5b7578569ca48b0dac5e3688e17818f02614627d907349ef8887b3.png)

The graph above represents the hourly cost of a boat ride at a certain lake. What is the actual cost of a boat ride?
questions.worked_solution:
The graph has a $y$-intercept at $(0,20),$ which means that the cost is $$20$ even when no time has been elapsed. So, the boat rental charges an initial fee of $$20.00.$

To find the cost per hour, notice that the units of the slope are

$$
\frac{\text{dollars}}{\text{hours}},
$$

or dollars per hour. So, to calculate the cost per hour, we need to calculate the slope of the line. 

Since the line passes through the points $(0,20)$ and $(4,40)$, we find its slope as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}} \\  & =\frac{40-20}{4-0} \\  & =\frac{20}{4} \\  & =5\text{ dollars/hour}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the cost of a ride is $$20.00$ plus $$5.00$ per hour.

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating S(x,y) Using the Shortcut Formula
questions.worked_solution:
Given a set of $n$ paired observations ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ and ${y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{n},$ the sum of products of deviations from the means can be calculated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{xy} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i}{x}_{i}{y}_{i}-\frac{1}{n}({\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i})({\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{y}_{i})\end{aligned}
$$

First, we calculate the sum of the ${x}_{i}$ and ${y}_{i}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} & =1+7+3+4+6+10=31, \\ {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{y}_{i} & =11+3+7+2+1+18=42\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that ${\sum }_{i=1}^{6}{x}_{i}{y}_{i}=247.$

Finally, by substituting in the above formula, we get

$$
{S}_{xy}=247-\frac{1}{6}(31)(42)=247-217=30.
$$

First, notice that the horizontal asymptote of the graph is $y=2,$ while the vertical asymptote is $x=1.$ This means that $k=2$ and $b=1,$ and we can re-write our function as

$$
y=\frac{a}{x-1}+2.
$$

Also, we are given that the point $(2,5)$ lies on the graph. Substituting its coordinates into the equation above, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{a}{x-1}+2 \\ 5 & =\frac{a}{2-1}+2 \\ 3 & =\frac{a}{1} \\ a & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $a+b+k=3+1+2=6.$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Index of a Term Given Two Terms
questions.problem:
Given an arithmetic sequence that has $f(2)=5$ and $f(4)=23$, what is the index of the term $158?$

Answer: {{answer}}
questions.worked_solution:
To construct the formula for the sequence, we need to know the common difference $d$ and the first term $f(1).$

Since we are given $f(2)=5$ and $f(4)=23,$ we can find the common difference by dividing the total difference by the number of jumps:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\frac{f(4)-f(2)}{4-2} \\  & =\frac{23-5}{4-2} \\  & =\frac{18}{2} \\  & =9\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(2)=5$ is $1$ jump after $f(1),$ we can determine the first term of the sequence:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2) & =f(1)+d \\ 5 & =f(1)+9 \\ -4 & =f(1)\end{aligned}
$$

So, the formula for the $n$th term is:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(n) & =f(1)+(n-1)d \\  & =-4+(n-1)(9) \\  & =-4+9n-9 \\  & =9n-13\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for the value of $n$ that gives $f(n)=158,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(n) & =9n-13 \\ 158 & =9n-13 \\ 171 & =9n \\ \frac{171}{9} & =n \\ 19 & =n\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $158$ is the $19$th term of the sequence.

questions.knowledge_point: Solving Two-Step Equations
questions.worked_solution:
In part 1, we found that $p(5)=25a+5b.$ So, we need to solve the equation $25a+5b=375$ for the parameter $b.$

We need to isolate the variable $b.$ To do this, we treat $a$ as though it were a constant and apply the addition and multiplication principles as usual.

First, we subtract $25a$ from both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}25a+5b & =375 \\ 25a+5b-25a & =375-25a \\ 5b & =375-25a\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we divide both sides of the equation by $5:$

$$
\begin{aligned}5b & =375-25a \\ \frac{5b}{5} & =\frac{375-25a}{5} \\ \frac{\cancel{5}b}{\cancel{5}} & =\frac{375}{5}-\frac{25a}{5} \\ b & =75-5a\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $b=75-5a.$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving a System of Linear Equations Using Substitution
questions.worked_solution:
We have the following system of linear equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}b=75-5a \\ 70a+9b=600\end{aligned}
$$

We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. 

Notice that the first equation is already solved for $b:$

$$
b=75-5a
$$

So, we replace $b$ in the second equation and solve for $a:$

$$
\begin{aligned}70a+9b & =600 \\ 70a+9(75-5a) & =600 \\ 70a+675-45a & =600 \\ 25a+675 & =600 \\ 25a & =-75 \\ a & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute $a=-3$ into $b=75-5a,$ we can then find the value of $b:$

$$
\begin{aligned}b & =75-5(-3) \\ b & =90\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $a=-3,\,b=90.$

$$

questions.knowledge_point: Factoring Trinomials With Positive Coefficients
questions.problem:
Find the minimum number of luxury white chocolate boxes the company needs to produce per day to make a daily profit of $$600.$

The company needs to produce$\,$
{{field-1}}$\,$ luxury white chocolate boxes per day.
questions.worked_solution:
From part 5, the required number of white chocolate boxes $x$ is the solution to the equation

$$
3\cdot ({x}^{2}-30x+200)=0.
$$

Dividing this equation by $3,$ we have

$$
{x}^{2}-30x+200=0.
$$

To solve this equation, we want to find a factor pair of the constant term $(200)$ that also adds up to the coefficient of the linear term $(-30).$ The required factors are $(-10)$ and $(-20).$

Using this factor pair, we write the linear term as $-30x=-10x-20x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-30x+200 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-10x-20x+200 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we factor the first two terms and the last two terms separately and then factor the expression completely:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-10x-20x+200 & =0 \\ ({x}^{2}-10x)+(-20x+200) & =0 \\ x(x-10)-20(x-10) & =0 \\ (x-10)(x-20)\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the solutions are $x=10$ or $x=20.$ Since we require the minimum solution, we conclude that the company needs to produce $10$ luxury white chocolate boxes per day to make a profit of $$600.$

questions.knowledge_point: Converting a Recursive Formula to an Explicit Formula
questions.problem:
The company wants to increase its output by implementing a new production model. The number of luxury white chocolate boxes ${a}_{n}$ produced on the $n$th day since the implementation of the new model is given by the arithmetic sequence

$$
{a}_{n+1}={a}_{n}+5,\,{a}_{1}=10,\,n\ge 1
$$

What is the explicit formula for the $n$th term of this arithmetic sequence?

${a}_{n}=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
The explicit formula for the $n$th term of an arithmetic sequence is

$$
{a}_{n}={a}_{1}+(n-1)d,\,n\ge 1,
$$

so we need to determine the first term ${a}_{1}$ and the common difference $d.$

We are given that the first term is ${a}_{1}=10,$ and we can use the recursive rule to compute the second term as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} & ={a}_{1}+5 \\  & =10+5 \\  & =15\end{aligned}
$$

Using the first and second terms, we can compute the common difference:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & ={a}_{2}-{a}_{1} \\  & =15-10 \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Now we substitute ${a}_{1}=10$ and $d=5$ into the formula for the $n$th term:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}+(n-1)d \\  & =10+(n-1)(5) \\  & =10+5n-5 \\  & =5n+5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the formula for the $n$th term is

$$
{a}_{n}=5n+5,\,n\ge 1.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Unit Vector Parallel to a Given Vector
questions.problem: Let $a=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ and $b=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 8\end{aligned}].$ Find a unit vector that is parallel to $2a+b$ and points the same direction.
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that to find a unit vector that is parallel to a given vector and points the same direction, we need to divide the given vector by its length:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =\frac{2a+b}{|2a+b|}\end{aligned}
$$

First, let's compute the sum:

$$
\begin{aligned}2a+b & =2\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 4\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0+5 \\ 4+8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 12\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula for the magnitude of a vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|2a+b| & =\sqrt{{5}^{2}+{12}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{169} \\  & =13.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we divide $2a+b$ by its length and get the following unit vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =\frac{2a+b}{|2a+b|} \\  & =\frac{1}{13}(2a+b) \\  & =\frac{1}{13}\cdot [\begin{aligned}5 \\ 12\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{13} \\ \frac{12}{13}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Applying the Rules of Sum and Product With Letter and Digits
questions.problem:
A word consists of $3$ letters, as shown below:

| Letter | Letter | Letter |
| --- | --- | --- |

Here, each "Letter" can be any capital from A-H ($8$ in total). How many possible words are there?
questions.worked_solution:
For each letter, there is a total of $8$ possibilities: A, B, C, D, E, F, G, and H.

Using the **rule of product**, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Number of words} & =\text{Number of options in the first slot} \\  & \times \text{Number of options in the second slot} \\  & \times \text{Number of options in the third slot} \\  & =8\times 8\times 8 \\  & ={8}^{3} \\  & =512.\end{aligned}
$$

So, there are $512$ possible words.

questions.knowledge_point: Estimating Using Probabilities
questions.problem:
A group of randomly selected students from Chicago High School was asked which country they want to visit between Brazil, Spain, France, or Japan. The results of the survey are summarized in the two-way frequency table below.

|  | Brazil | Spain | France | Japan | Totals |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Girls | $12$ | $20$ | $9$ | $14$ | $55$ |
| Boys | $14$ | $10$ | $20$ | $1$ | $45$ |
| Totals | $26$ | $30$ | $29$ | $15$ | $100$ |

Boston High School has $400$ students. Assuming that the distribution of the results is the same in both high schools, estimate the number of girls at Boston High School who wish to visit Brazil or France. Round your answer to the nearest integer.
questions.worked_solution:
To estimate the number of girls who wish to visit Brazil or France, we

- add up the numbers in the intersection of the row **"Girls"** and the column **"Brazil"** and the intersection of the row **"Girls"** and the column **"France"**, and then

- divide by the total number of data points in the table.

|  | Brazil | Spain | France | Japan | Totals |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Girls | $12$ | $20$ | $9$ | $14$ | $55$ |
| Boys | $14$ | $10$ | $20$ | $1$ | $45$ |
| Totals | $26$ | $30$ | $29$ | $15$ | $100$ |

Adding up these numbers and then dividing by the total number of data points in the table $(100),$ we get

$$
p=\frac{12+9}{100}=\frac{21}{100}=0.21.
$$

This represents the estimated probability that a randomly selected student is a girl who wishes to visit Brazil or France.

Finally, to find the estimated number of girls of Boston High School who wish to visit Brazil or France, we multiply the total number of students in Boston High School $(400)$ by the probability above:

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =400\cdot p \\  & =400\cdot 0.21 \\  & =84\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating an Expression Involving Powers of i Using the Laws of Exponents
questions.worked_solution:
Using the power law for exponents, we have

$$
{a}^{4}={({\text{i}}^{2})}^{4}={\text{i}}^{2\cdot 4}={\text{i}}^{8}.
$$

To find the value of $\text{i}$ raised to some positive integer power $n$, we divide $n$ by $4,$ and raise $\text{i}$ to the remainder.

In our case, we have $n=8.$ Dividing the power by $4,$ we get

$$
8÷4=2\,\text{R}0.
$$

So the remainder is $0.$ Therefore,

$$
{\text{i}}^{8}={\text{i}}^{0}=1.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating the Sum or Difference of Two Functions
questions.worked_solution:
The notation $(f-g)(x)$ means the difference of the functions $f(x)$ and $g(x).$ 

**Method 1** 

To evaluate $(f-g)(4),$ we find $f(4)$ and $g(4),$ and then subtract $g(4)$ from $f(4).$

So, first we find $f(4)$ and $g(4):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(4) & =(4)^{2}-6=10 \\ g(4) & =-(4)+2=-2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Next, we subtract $g(4)$ from $f(4)$:

$$
(f-g)(4)=f(4)-g(4)=10-(-2)=12
$$

**Method 2**

First we find the difference of the two functions $f$ and $g$ by subtracting $g(x)$ from $f(x)$: 

$$
\begin{aligned}(f-g)(x) & =({x}^{2}-6)-(-x+2) \\  & ={x}^{2}-6+x-2 \\  & ={x}^{2}+x-8\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate $(f-g)(4):$

$$
\begin{aligned}(f-g)(4) & =(4)^{2}+4-8=12\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Let's calculate ${log}_{12}(23)$ by changing the base $12$ to the common logarithm (base $10$).

We use the change of base formula:

$$
{log}_{a}X=\frac{{log}_{b}X}{{log}_{b}a}
$$

In our case, $a=12,$ $X=23,$ $b=10.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{12}(23) & =\frac{{log}_{10}(23)}{{log}_{10}(12)} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{log}(23)}{\operatorname{log}(12)} \\  & \approx \frac{1.361\,728}{1.079\,181} \\  & \approx 1.262\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Terms of a Fibonacci Sequence Given in Function Notation
questions.problem:
Consider the following sequence:

$$
f(n+2)=f(n+1)+f(n)\,,\,f(1)=3\,,\,f(2)=-1,\,n\ge 1
$$

The fourth term of the sequence is{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
The fourth term is represented by $f(4).$

To compute $f(4),$ we first need to compute $f(3).$ So, we substitute $n=1$ into the recursive formula, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1+2) & =f(1+1)+f(1) \\ f(3) & =f(2)+f(1) \\ f(3) & =(-1)+3 \\ f(3) & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Next, to compute $f(4),$ we substitute $n=2$ into the recursive formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2+2) & =f(2+1)+f(2) \\ f(4) & =f(3)+f(2) \\ f(4) & =2+(-1) \\ f(4) & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the fourth term of the sequence is $f(4)=1.$

questions.problem: Three balls are drawn from a bag that contains $5$ white balls and $4$ black balls. Define $A$ to be the event "at least one white ball is drawn." It is known that $P(A)=0.95$ to $2$ decimal places. To two decimal places, what is the probability of drawing three black balls?
questions.worked_solution:
The event "three black balls are drawn" is the opposite of the event "at least one white ball is drawn."

So, the event "three black balls are drawn" is the complement of $A,$ denoted ${A}^{'}.$

Since we know that $P(A)=0.95$ to $2$ decimal places, we can calculate $P({A}^{'})$ using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A)+P({A}^{'}) & =1 \\ P({A}^{'}) & =1-P(A) \\  & =1-0.95 \\  & =0.05.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying True Statements Regarding an Event and its Complement
questions.problem:
Two fair $6$-sided dice are rolled. Define $A$ to be the event "the sum of outcomes is equal to $5.$" Which of the following statements are true regarding this event?

I. - $P(A)=0.15$ to $2$ decimal places
II. - ${A}^{'}$ is the event "the sum of the outcomes is less than $5$"
III. - $P({A}^{'})=0.89$ to $2$ decimal places
questions.worked_solution:
Let's inspect each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. There are $36$ possible outcomes and $4$ of these have the sum of the outcomes equal to $5,$ namely $(1,4),(4,1),(2,3),(3,2).$ Therefore,

$$
P(A)=\frac{4}{36}=0.11
$$

to $2$ decimal places.

- Statement II is false. The complement of $A$ is the event ${A}^{'},$ "the sum of the outcomes is not equal to $5.$

- Statement III is true. Since we know that $P(A)=0.11$ to $2$ decimal places, we can calculate $P({A}^{'})$ using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A)+P({A}^{'}) & =1 \\ P({A}^{'}) & =1-P(A) \\  & =1-0.11 \\  & =0.89.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

$$

to $2$ decimal places.

- Statement III is true. Since we know that $P(A)=0.42$ to $2$ decimal places, we can calculate $P({A}^{'})$ using the formula

$$

questions.problem: If $\frac{16a-8}{4}$ is written in the form $pa+q,$ what are the values of $p$ and $q?$
questions.worked_solution:
Splitting the fraction into separate terms and then simplifying the fractions in the individual terms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{16a-8}{4} & = \\ \frac{16a}{4}-\frac{8}{4} & = \\ \frac{16}{4}\cdot a-2 & = \\ 4a-2 & .\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above in the form $pa+qb,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{{(4)}_{⏟}}_{p}a+{{(-2)}_{⏟}}_{q}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=4$ and $q=-2.$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying the Global Minimum of a Function

First, we recall the following definitions:

* The global minimum of a function is the smallest value that the function attains on its domain. There can only be (at most) one global minimum.

* A global minimum point of a function is a point $(x,y)$ where a function reaches a global minimum. There can be zero, one, or many global minimum points.

For our function, the minimum value reached by the function is $h(x)=-2.$

Therefore, the global minimum is ${h}_{min}=-2.$ The function reaches this value when $x=1,$ so the global minimum point is $(1,-2).$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing an Inverse Function Using the Definition
questions.worked_solution:
If $r$ is the inverse of $g,$ then 

$$
r(g(x))=x.
$$

To find $r(g(x)),$ we write down the function $r$ and replace every occurrence of $x$ with $g(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(x) & =\frac{1}{3}x+k \\ r(g(x)) & =\frac{1}{3}g(x)+k\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $g(x)=3x-1$ into the right-hand side of our expression and simplify, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(g(x)) & =\frac{1}{3}g(x)+k \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(3x-1)+k \\  & =x-\frac{1}{3}+k\end{aligned}
$$

However, we know that $r(g(x))=x.$ Equating the expression above with $x$ and solving for $k$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}r(g(x)) & =x \\ x-\frac{1}{3}+k & =x \\ \cancel{x}-\frac{1}{3}+k & =\cancel{x} \\ -\frac{1}{3}+k & =0 \\ k & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: $\operatorname{cos}({270}^{∘})+\operatorname{sin}({180}^{∘})=${{field-1}}

The angles ${180}^{∘}$ and ${270}^{∘}$ are quadrantal angles. Let's draw out the quadrantal angles on the unit circle.

- Let's first consider the angle ${270}^{∘}.$ From the unit circle, we see that the angle ${270}^{∘}$ corresponds to the point $(0,-1).$ Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the $x$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{cos}({270}^{∘})=0.$

- Now, let's consider the angle ${180}^{∘}.$ From the unit circle, we see that the angle ${180}^{∘}$ corresponds to the point $(-1,0).$ Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the $y$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{sin}({180}^{∘})=0.$

Finally, we get

$$
\operatorname{cos}({270}^{∘})+\operatorname{sin}({180}^{∘})=0+0=0.
$$

$$
\operatorname{tan}({270}^{∘})=\frac{\operatorname{sin}({270}^{∘})}{\operatorname{cos}({270}^{∘})}=\frac{-1}{0}.
$$

However, division by zero is undefined. Therefore, $\operatorname{tan}({270}^{∘})$ is undefined.

questions.problem:
Find the value of $\operatorname{tan}\pi +\operatorname{cot}(\frac{\pi }{2}).$

Answer: {{answer}}
questions.worked_solution:
The angles $\pi $ and $\frac{\pi }{2}$ are quadrantal angles. Let's draw out the quadrantal angles on the unit circle.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/history-question-import-2026-10-04/import-ready/assets/792a778286533d589a3410223aaf197b07e64ea77566042d7bb8ac13fbad9768.png)

Let's first consider the angle $\pi .$ From the unit circle, we see that the angle $\pi $ corresponds to the point $(-1,0).$

- Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the $x$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{cos}\pi =-1.$

- Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the $y$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{sin}\pi =0.$

Therefore, using the fact that $\operatorname{tan}\theta =\frac{\operatorname{sin}\theta }{\operatorname{cos}\theta },$ we have

$$
\operatorname{tan}\pi =\frac{\operatorname{sin}\pi }{\operatorname{cos}\pi }=\frac{0}{-1}=0.
$$

Now, let's consider the angle $\frac{\pi }{2}.$ From the unit circle, we see that the angle $\frac{\pi }{2}$ corresponds to the point $(0,1).$

- Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the $x$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{cos}(\frac{\pi }{2})=0.$

- Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the $y$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{2})=1.$

Therefore, using the fact that $\operatorname{cot}\theta =\frac{\operatorname{cos}\theta }{\operatorname{sin}\theta },$ we have

$$
\operatorname{cot}(\frac{\pi }{2})=\frac{\operatorname{cos}(\frac{\pi }{2})}{\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{2})}=\frac{0}{1}=0.
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\operatorname{tan}\pi +\operatorname{cot}(\frac{\pi }{2})=0+0=0.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Point That Lies on a Transformed Curve
questions.problem: The point $(a,b)$ lies on the curve $y={x}^{3}.$ Which of the following points **must** lie on $y=2(x+2)^{3}?$
questions.worked_solution:
**Method 1**

To plot $y=2(x+2)^{3},$ we apply the following steps:

- First, we take the graph $y={x}^{3}.$

- Then, we shift the graph horizontally by $2$ units to the left and get the graph of $y=(x+2)^{3}.$ After this transformation, the point $(a,b)$ will be mapped to the point

$$
(a-2,b).
$$

- Finally, we stretch the graph by a scale factor of  $2$ parallel to the $y$ -axis and get the graph of  $y=2(x+2)^{3}.$ After this transformation, the point $(a-2,b)$ will be mapped to the point 

$$
(a-2,2b).
$$

**Method 2**

Since the point $(a,b)$ lies on the graph of $y={x}^{3}$, we have that ${a}^{3}=b.$

Now consider the graph of $y=2(x+2)^{3}.$ Substituting $x=a-2$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =2(a-2+2)^{3} \\  & =2{a}^{3} \\  & =2b.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the point $(a-2,2b)$ must lie on $y=2(x+2)^{3}.$

- Then, we shift the graph horizontally by $1$ unit to the right and get the graph of $y=\sqrt{x-1}.$ After this transformation, the point $(a,b)$ will be mapped to the point

$$
(a+1,b).
$$

- Finally, we shift the result vertically by $1$ unit down and obtain the graph of $y=\sqrt{x-1}-1.$ After this transformation, the point $(a+1,b)$ will be mapped to the point

$$
(a+1,b-1).
$$

**Method 2**

Since the point $(a,b)$ lies on the graph of $y=\sqrt{x}$, we have that $\sqrt{a}=b.$

Now consider the graph of $y=\sqrt{x-1}-1.$ Substituting $x=a+1$, we get

$$

questions.problem: The point  $(0,4)$ lies on the curve $y=f(x)+2.$ Which of the following points **must** lie on $y=-f(x)-3?$
questions.worked_solution:
**Method 1**

To plot $y=-f(x)-3,$ we apply the following steps: 

- First, take the graph $y=f(x)+2.$

- Then, we shift the graph vertically by $2$ unit down and get the graph of $y=f(x).$ After this transformation, the point $(0,4)$ will be mapped to the point

$$
(0,4-2)=(0,2).
$$

- Next, we reflect the result across the $x$-axis and get the graph of $y=-f(x).$ After this transformation, the point $(0,2)$ will be mapped  to the point

$$
(0,-(2))=(0,-2).
$$

- Finally, shift the result vertically by $3$ units down and obtain the graph of $y=-f(x)-3.$ After this transformation, the point $(0,-2)$ will be mapped to the point 

$$
(0,-2-3)=(0,-5).
$$

**Method 2**

Since the point $(0,4)$ lies on the graph of $y=f(x)+2$, we have that 

$$
f(0)+2=4\,⟹\,f(0)=2.
$$

Now consider the graph of $y=-f(x)-3.$ Substituting $x=0$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-f(0)-3 \\  & =-2-3 \\  & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the point $(0,-5)$ must lie on $y=-f(x)-3.$

$$
(-1,3+2)=(-1,5).

$$

$$

Notice that the graph of $y=3f(\frac{x}{2})$ can be obtained from the graph of $y=f(x)$ by 

- stretching it by a scale factor of $2$ parallel to the $x$-axis, and then

- stretching it by a scale factor of $3$ parallel to the $y$-axis.

Since these transformations do not flip the graph across the $x$-axis, the combined transformation maps the local maximum of $y=f(x)$ to the local maximum of $y=3f(\frac{x}{2}).$ So, we need to find the image of $(-2,-1),$ the local maximum of $y=f(x),$ under the transformation. 

To plot $y=3f(\frac{x}{2}),$ we apply the following steps: 

- First, we take the graph $y=f(x)$ that passes through $(-2,-1).$

- Then, we  stretch the graph  along the $x$-axis by a scale factor of $2$ and get the graph of $y=f(\frac{x}{2}).$ After this transformation, the point $(-2,-1)$ will be mapped to the point

$$
(2\cdot (-2),-1)=(-4,-1).
$$

- Finally, we stretch the result  along the $y$-axis by a scale factor of $3$ and get the graph of $y=3f(\frac{x}{2}).$ After this transformation, the point $(-4,-1)$ will be mapped to the point

$$
(-4,3\cdot (-1))=(-4,-3).
$$

Therefore, the local maximum of $y=3f(\frac{x}{2})$ is $(-4,-3).$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving Two-Step Equations
questions.worked_solution:
In part 1, we found that $p(10)=100a+10b.$ So, we need to solve the equation $100a+10b=4\,800$ for the parameter $b.$

We need to isolate the variable $b.$ To do this, we treat $a$ as though it were a constant and apply the addition and multiplication principles as usual.

First, we subtract $100a$ from both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}100a+10b & =4\,800 \\ 100a+10b-100a & =4\,800-100a \\ 10b & =4\,800-100a\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we divide both sides of the equation by $10:$

$$
\begin{aligned}10b & =4\,800-100a \\ \frac{10b}{10} & =\frac{4\,800-100a}{10} \\ \frac{\cancel{10}b}{\cancel{10}} & =\frac{4\,800}{10}-\frac{100a}{10} \\ b & =480-10a\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $b=480-10a.$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving a System of Linear Equations Using Substitution
questions.worked_solution:
We have the following system of linear equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}b=480-10a \\ 20b+400a=7\,200\end{aligned}
$$

We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. 

Notice that the first equation is already solved for $b:$

$$
b=480-10a
$$

So, we replace $b$ in the second equation and solve for $a:$

$$
\begin{aligned}20b+400a & =7\,200 \\ 20(480-10a)+400a & =7\,200 \\ 9\,600-200a+400a & =7\,200 \\ 9\,600+200a & =7\,200 \\ 200a & =-2\,400 \\ a & =-12\end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute $a=-12$ into $b=480-10a,$ we can then find the value of $b:$

$$
\begin{aligned}b & =480-10(-12) \\ b & =600\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $a=-12,\,b=600.$

questions.problem:

Computing the GCF, we get

$$

Then, we rewrite each term in the original expression as a product with the $\text{GCF}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}12{x}^{2}-600x+7\,200 & = \\ 12\cdot ({x}^{2})+12\cdot (-50x)+12\cdot (600)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the $\text{GCF}$ outside the parentheses and keep the remaining terms inside:

$$
\begin{aligned}12\cdot ({x}^{2})+12\cdot (-50x)+12\cdot (600) & = \\ 12({x}^{2}-50x+600)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the missing expression is ${x}^{2}-50x+600.$

questions.knowledge_point: Factoring Trinomials With Positive Coefficients
questions.problem:
Find the minimum number of couches the company needs to produce per week to make a weekly profit of $$7\,200.$

The company needs to produce$\,$
{{field-1}}$\,$ couches per week.
questions.worked_solution:
From part 5, the required number of sofas $x$ is the solution to the equation

$$
12\cdot ({x}^{2}-50x+600)=0.
$$

Dividing this equation by $12,$ we have

$$
{x}^{2}-50x+600=0.
$$

To solve this equation, we want to find a factor pair of the constant term $(600)$ that also adds up to the coefficient of the linear term $(-50).$ The required factors are $(-20)$ and $(-30).$

Using this factor pair, we write the linear term as $-50x=-20x-30x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-50x+600 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-20x-30x+600 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we factor the first two terms and the last two terms separately and then factor the expression completely:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-20x-30+600 & =0 \\ ({x}^{2}-20x)+(-30x+600) & =0 \\ x(x-20)-30(x-20) & =0 \\ (x-30)(x-20) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the solutions are $x=20$ or $x=30.$ Since we require the minimum solution, we conclude that the company needs to produce $20$ couches per week to make a profit of $$7\,200.$

questions.knowledge_point: Converting a Recursive Formula to an Explicit Formula
questions.problem:
The company wants to increase its output by implementing a new production model. The number of couches ${a}_{n}$ produced in the $n$th week since the implementation of the new model is given by the arithmetic sequence

$$
{a}_{n+1}={a}_{n}+3,\,{a}_{1}=11,\,n\ge 1
$$

What is the explicit formula for the $n$th term of this arithmetic sequence?

${a}_{n}=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
The explicit formula for the $n$th term of an arithmetic sequence is

$$
{a}_{n}={a}_{1}+(n-1)d,\,n\ge 1,
$$

so we need to determine the first term ${a}_{1}$ and the common difference $d.$

We are given that the first term is ${a}_{1}=11,$ and we can use the recursive rule to compute the second term as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} & ={a}_{1}+3 \\  & =11+3 \\  & =14\end{aligned}
$$

Using the first and second terms, we can compute the common difference:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & ={a}_{2}-{a}_{1} \\  & =14-11 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Now we substitute ${a}_{1}=11$ and $d=3$ into the formula for the $n$th term:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}+(n-1)d \\  & =11+(n-1)(3) \\  & =11+3n-3 \\  & =3n+8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the formula for the $n$th term is

$$
{a}_{n}=3n+8,\,n\ge 1.
$$
